An upward planar drawing of a directed graph assigns positions to its vertices within a 2D plane and routes its edges via upward-directed piecewise-linear paths, maintaining that no edges cross one another. A graph is classified as upward planar if it admits such a drawing. This research examines the problems of determining upward planarity and enumerating all such drawings, focusing on specific parameterized models. First, we establish a fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) algorithm for the decision problem parameterized by the size of a directed acyclic subgraph that retains the original graph's diameter. This approach generalizes previous results derived from planar digraphs with out-degrees not exceeding one. Subsequently, we introduce an algorithm with running time $2^{O(\text{pathwidth})} \cdot n^{O(1)}$ for parameterizing by pathwidth, effectively solving the decision problem in parameterized fashion relative to this metric. Regarding the enumeration of all valid drawings, we present a kernelization technique for pathwidth; this limits the instance size to a function of the pathwidth parameter and can generate all upward planar drawings of instances within this parameter bound in linear time.

Humans frequently utilize memory to guide actions toward unfamiliar goals, such as navigating environments. This paper investigates the challenge of selecting which environmental fragments to retain within memory specifically for navigation. We demonstrate that the optimal set to memorize is highly context-dependent on the specific navigation task at hand. Furthermore, we introduce MemoNav, an in-memory agent capable of recalling and visually re-examining stored fragments during navigation. By employing various image representations of these stored fragments—ranging from global views to local perspectives—MemoNav can achieve navigation success in previously seen scenarios. We also present an efficient method to compute diverse visual fragment representations for retention. Extensive experiments confirm that MemoNav surpasses standard, amnesiac navigation agents and existing approaches that rely solely on memory of the immediate surroundings.

Cellular networks have evolved continuously since their inception, a trajectory that will persist into the future. This paper examines the historical development of the mobile cell concept, analyzes current advancements, and explores future directions. It provides an overview of the evolution of base stations from 4G through projected future iterations, offering a forward-looking analysis of their evolution to AI-driven, AI-integrated, and AI-enabled small cells for upcoming 6G systems.

This paper introduces a new framework for modeling dynamics on hypergraphs and its limit graphs, demonstrating the approach's utility through two specific applications: a coloring problem and a framework for hypernomial expansion.

The expectation values of single-trace operators within a conformal field theory, arranged by their classical dimension and quantum corrections, generate a bivariate power series known as the operator expansion (exp). This framework reveals a non-trivial relationship with the topological expansion employed in string theory, where coefficients organize themselves according to an asymptotic structure governed by Bell polynomials. Consequently, this suggests that the topological series can be completely derived from the expectation value data of single-trace operators.

Direct breakup of the $^{16}$O nucleus into an alpha particle and $^{12}$C yields the Hoyle state via direct decay to two alphas. This process offers a promising method for evaluating the direct-decay component of the width for the Hoyle state in the 2$_{+}$ state of $^{12}$C. This study reports the initial results from an experiment at TRIUMPH utilizing a Time Projection Chamber (TPC) to analyze this direct decay. By employing a novel technique for analyzing TPC data, we achieved nearly background-free observation of the three-body final state, consisting of three alphas and a recoil of $^{12}$C. This approach enables the precise determination of the direct-decay matrix element for the Hoyle state without requiring a nuclear target. Consequently, we derived the value of the direct-decay term for the width of the Hoyle state as $\Gamma_{\rm dd} = 0.20^{+0.13}_{-0.10}$ eV, with systematic uncertainties being negligible.

This study examines oscillatory and tip-splitting instabilities within two-dimensional dynamic brittle fracture using a phase-field framework. The findings reveal that both inherent material length scales and stress singularities influence the onset of these instabilities. Furthermore, a material-specific critical cone angle is identified; when the fracture energy dissipation angle falls below this critical value, oscillatory instability cannot develop. The research also quantifies how material parameters and conical crack geometry dictate the critical loading levels required to trigger either oscillatory or tip-dividing failures. Notably, under conditions of minimal energy dissipation angles and tip-dividing onset, the resulting radius is governed exclusively by initial values set at the time of instability initiation.

This work investigates communication across distributed systems subject to finite-state interference, where a channel encoder must determine the appropriate interference state before encoding, relying on an initial feedback channel for state observation. Assuming the channel encoder is state-aware and that this initial feedback channel possesses sufficient capacity, we demonstrate that the feedback channel's capacity is identical to that of the main channel augmented with non-causal side information, even in the presence of a finite-state interference model. We provide lower and upper bounds for the interference state Markov chain and establish that the described feedback mechanism requires only a feedback channel capacity marginally exceeding that of the primary link to enable the one-time acquisition of the interference state.

We investigate superfluidity in two-dimensional cold atoms with Rashba spin-orbit coupling exposed to an external magnetic field, focusing on the low-density regime where mean-field theory predicts a magnetized Berezinskii-Poskarov-Zhitninskii (Berezinskii) state. By employing density matrix renormalization group techniques, we examine spin-singlet pairing superfluids featuring both chiral and gapped order parameters. Our findings reveal that, contrary to expectations, the ground state frequently adopts a spin-singlet superfluid characterized by a gapped excitation spectrum with no chirality, even at lower interactions. This ground state competes with both the singlet Berezinskii state and the previously noted triplet state; however, this gapped singlet phase demonstrates robustness across a broader spectrum of interaction parameters. Furthermore, we explore the capacity to induce a chiral component in this gapped singlet phase through specific modifications to the interaction potential.

This paper details the submissions created for the SemEval-2021 Task 9: Truth Assessment and Evidence Retrieval for Tabular Data in Scientific Articles, alongside the employed annotation protocols and evaluation metrics. Our group presented two distinct pipelines: one dedicated to identifying textual proof within tables and another for verifying the validity of statements. Both were constructed using ensembles of deep neural networks enhanced with deep learning techniques.

Intricate numbers, first defined by the author, are characterized by two specific traits: their real component exceeds their imaginary component's magnitude, and their fractional part is irrational. This discussion examines the frequency of Intricate numbers among various non-rational quantum mechanical numbers found in standard curricula. Although these numbers often appear as mere abstract mathematical constructs with little perceived utility in that curriculum, their lack of usefulness is temporary. In the author's upcoming research, these numbers are set to play a significant role in research involving topological phases of matter and quantum information.

For a metric space $(V, d)$, a subset $S \subseteq V$ is termed a *shortened resolving set* for a specific vertex $v \in V$ if, for every pair of distinct vertices $x$ and $y$, the condition $|d(x, s) - d(y, s)| \neq 0$ holds for at least one $s \in S$ exclusively when either both $x$ and $y$ equal $v$, or one is in $S$ while the other is outside $S \cup \{v\}$. This subset minimizes size to be *shortened unique*, where its minimum possible size defines the *shortened metric dimension* of $v$ and the associated space. When dealing with graphs, this concept fixes the reference vertex at a degree-one node (a "leaf"). In this context, a shortened resolving set ensures that for any two non-adjacent vertices, their distances from set members differ by at least zero, whereas for adjacent vertices, this difference is strictly non-zero for at least one set element adjacent to it.

This study introduces novel mathematical formulations for simulating groundwater dynamics and water level changes, building upon prior research. While previous work established the equivalence of a first-order hyperbolic system with source terms to a second-order parabolic formulation involving a pressure-like variable, this paper extends that equivalence to formulations involving specific hydraulic potentials. It further demonstrates inter-equivalence among three formulations: (1) a second-order system of pressure differential equations, (2) a first-order system of pressure differential equations incorporating specific wave characteristics, and (3) a first-order system of pressure differential equations using an entropic variable formulation.

This study investigates the merging of ozone and ultraviolet (UV) radiation to create a compact, energy-efficient system for treating low-temperature flue gas with the goal of removing sulfur dioxide (SO₂). The research evaluates the impact of key parameters—including temperature, residence time, and UV radiation intensity—on the efficiency of SO₂ elimination. The findings indicate that a system combining UV radiation and ozone is a viable method for desulfurizing low-heat flue gas.

Driven by the need for efficient processing capable of handling intensive tasks like pattern recognition and classification, there has been a surge in interest regarding the design and implementation of neuromorphic systems. Systems utilizing artificial neurons and spiking communication for information transfer present an alternative computational model to traditional von Neumann architectures, offering superior performance for specific workloads. To streamline the development of these systems, it is essential to adopt industry-standard HDI-based virtual frameworks capable of emulating key features such as spiking communication and concurrent specialized operations. This paper introduces a new SystemC framework designed to accelerate the design space exploration of neuromorphic systems by providing realistic models of these core features, thereby allowing for fine-grained exploitation of advantages like low power consumption and enhanced throughput. Written in standard SystemC, the framework ensures broad hardware description language compatibility and facilitates integration into various HDL-based virtual environments.

Current machine learning models often lack the capacity to handle ambiguity in their output labels, a limitation that prevents their use in safety-critical domains like autonomous driving or healthcare. While existing research has explored how to train classifiers to produce sets of possible labels rather than single definitive ones, it has not adequately addressed scenarios involving uncertainty regarding the ambiguity itself—specifically, not knowing which type of ambiguity a particular label uncertainty represents. This work introduces "indecision forests," a novel algorithm capable of generating label sets and identifying the specific ambiguity category associated with each classification decision. We evaluated this approach on a practical ambiguity involving two alternative interpretations for identifying obstacles in autonomous vehicle safety. Empirical results indicate that indecision forests surpass existing methods in accuracy, computational speed, and interpretability.

Discrete Time Warping (DTW) is a widely used method for measuring the similarity between time series, yet its computational complexity scales cubically with the input length ($O(L^3)$), rendering it impractical for comparing long sequences. To mitigate this, various early discarding strategies have been developed to halt computation when a certain level of similarity is evident. This paper introduces PrunedDTW, an algorithm that achieves a significant four-fold speedup compared to standard DTW while maintaining identical similarity outcomes. Additionally, we present a similarity search algorithm capable of quickly identifying all matches within a predefined similarity threshold.

Testing represents a vital component of the software development lifecycle, yet few individuals within the software engineering field possess the necessary testing expertise. To enhance testing knowledge and competencies among software engineering graduates, various instructional techniques have been explored. This study compares two specific teaching methods: an inquiry-based instruction (IBI) approach featuring general conceptual guidance, and a conventional method (CDE) providing detailed, specific feedback. Conducted over one academic year with 132 participants, the research utilized pre- and post-tests to evaluate learning outcomes alongside a survey assessing student reactions. Results indicate that IBI is more effective than CDE for improving testing knowledge and that students respond more positively to IBI by valuing its problem-solving orientation and inquiry-based nature.

While Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) excel at high-precision tasks, their lack of transparency hinders trust among stakeholders, particularly in critical fields like medicine and law. To address this, our approach combines a specialized method with Inductive Logic Programming (ILP) concept learning to generate human-readable definitions for DNN inputs and outputs. Specifically, we employ a refined concept analysis technique that handles both nominal and numeric data, accommodating concepts with multiple attributes and handling conceptual hierarchies. Our human-centric framework decomposes a DNN's input space into a conceptual lattice, interprets the output associated with each node, and constructs a conceptual hierarchy that approximates the original DNN.

Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have become a popular tool for processing graph-structured data, yet their success hinges on an oversimplified view of convolution that ignores the non-stationary nature of graphs, creating a mismatch between theory and practice. This study investigates a critical limitation of the convolution operation in current graph signal processing approaches: "over-blurring." We demonstrate that this phenomenon occurs because GCN convolutions fail to adapt to specific frequency bands, leading to excessive smoothing of low-frequency components. Consequently, this inhibits effective recovery of graph attributes during supervised learning. To address these issues, we introduce the Over-blurring Blurring Network (OBN), which employs a novel "over-blurring" frequency filter. This mechanism enhances low-frequency resolution while offering superior generalization capabilities. Experimental results across multiple real-world datasets confirm that the proposed OBN significantly outperforms existing methods in handling the challenges posed to graph data processing.

This study reports a search for invisible or nearly invisible final states generated in association with a $Z$ boson, using proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s} =$ 13 TeV from the CMS experiment at the LHC. Data collected during 2016, 2017, and 2018, totaling an integrated luminosity of 137 fb$^{-1}$, were analyzed. The analysis targets a single isolated lepton (either an electron or a muon) alongside significant transverse momentum imbalance. Constraints on single-shadow production are established, yielding cross-section limits of 0.14 fb (95% C.L.) for shadows decaying into two photons, and 0.11 fb (95% C.L.) for shadows decaying into two hadronic jets. These findings constrain several theoretical models, including lepton universality-violating lepton flavor violation, two-Higgs-doublet models, and shadows arising from dark sectors.

Although Transverse Momentum-Dependent (TMD) and Wormlight (WGD) frameworks have been extensively studied, this paper introduces new characteristics for $k_\perp$-dependent parton distributions. These properties are grounded in the Lorentz and Poincaré symmetries, alongside time-reversal ($T$) and charge-conjugation ($C$) invariances. First, leveraging Lorentz symmetry, we demonstrate that helicity-dependent distributions can be simplified, reducing the number of independent functions from three to 2. Second, using Poincaré invariances, we show that the distribution describing unpolarized quark transverse motion reduces its dependence on the light-cone variable $x$ from two to a single function. Third, by applying charge-conjugation ($C$) and time-reversal ($T$) invariances, we prove that the transversity distribution for an unpolarized hadron vanishes. These theoretical results are consistent with standard TMD and WGD analyses.

In this paper, we investigate spaces equipped with "stockings"—topological group topologies that remain unchanged under the action of a specific subgroup of the automorphism group of the group itself. We demonstrate that the class of space with stockings forms a proper category that is closed with respect to the formation of uniform colimits. Furthermore, we provide several additional properties and examples related to these spaces.

The discovery of the giant magnetoresistance effect in magnetic B2Heusler alloys has reignited interest in developing high-quality epitaxial layers of these materials on various substrates. This study introduces a method to characterize the growth modes of B2Heusler alloys using reflection high-energy electron diffraction (RHEEED) and atomic force microscopy (AFM). The findings reveal a transition from distant, island-based (Volmer-Weber) growth to a layer-by-layer (Stranski-Krastanov) mechanism as the B2Heusler composition shifts from Co-based to Fe-based variants. Additionally, the research identifies two critical parameters that dictate growth mode: the intrinsic B2Heusler lattice constant and the magnitude of both van der Waals and pinhole interactions relative to lattice mismatch. The study further demonstrates how these factors can be manipulated to optimize film morphology.

This paper introduces a new class of non-stationary multivariate time series models, the non-stationary integrated autoregressive moving average with constant mean (CIARMA(c,q)) model, which features innovations following a symmetric generalized hypergeometric distribution (SGH). These CIARMA models exhibit robust hypergeometric innovations capable of producing autocorrelations and spectra that decay polynomially at large lags, allowing for the analysis of real-world datasets with both robust tail behaviors and non-stationarity. Although standard statistical inference techniques for such data exist in the stationary setting, they fail under non-stationarity due to the absence of ergodicity. Consequently, this study establishes consistent estimators for CIARMA model parameters alongside their asymptotic distributions.

The JWST PEARLS survey, a new initiative targeting the most massive galaxy clusters in the early universe, has recently released its initial findings. This paper details the observational strategy and presents the first catalog of 1000+ red supergiant (RSG) stars located within cluster environments at redshifts $z \in [0.3, 0.5]$. The study identifies approximately 1000 RSG candidates by leveraging JWST's superior near-infrared sensitivity and spectral resolution, utilizing the RSG-specific near-infrared bump as a robust selection criterion. We cross-referenced these candidates with existing databases to determine their binary status and measured their physical parameters, including effective temperatures, masses, and ages, using the PHOENIX spectral synthesis code. The resulting RSG population exhibits a wide variety of effective temperatures, ranging from 2,000 K to 2,500 K, with masses between 10 and 25 solar masses, and ages of roughly 100 million years. We also calculated the total number of RSGs within cluster galaxies, estimating $N_{\rm RSG} = 10^3$ with a significant uncertainty of 0.5 dex. Furthermore, we identified a unique early-type RSG candidate (J0102-4915) exhibiting a spectral type of B2.5 and an effective temperature of 13,000

This study examines a partnership between a content provider (CP) and an internet service provider (ISP), focusing on how to distribute profits effectively. The CP, which operates multiple data centers (DCs) globally, seeks to establish direct billing with ISPs to foster better service quality. The proposed profit distribution framework utilizes a Shapley value function to determine each ISP's specific contribution to the CP's total revenue. Numerical evaluations demonstrate that this approach encourages content providers to engage with higher-capacity ISPs and motivates ISPs to invest in enhanced network quality.

This study introduces a pair of adjunctions linking the category of algebras over commutative base rings to that of unital vector spaces, specifically utilizing 2-categories. One direction maps a commutative ring $R$-algebra $\mathfrak{a}$ to its spectrum $\mathrm{Spec}(\mathfrak{a})$, interpreted as an affine scheme enriched with its associated vector spaces of invariants under the action of $\mathfrak{a}$. The reverse maps a given scheme $X$ to the collection of its global sections. These concepts are illustrated through an example involving a "quantum plane" and its classical counterpart.

The $\alpha$-attractor framework has become a leading approach for investigating inflationary cosmology, largely due to its ability to yield significant analytical progress. This study introduces a novel expansion technique within the $\alpha$-attractor model, enabling precise and efficient calculations of inflationary observables near the end of inflation. We demonstrate this method using both exponential and $SU(2)$-invariant models. Furthermore, we compare our results with those derived through the slow-roll approximation and numerical simulations. The proposed expansion proves particularly advantageous for scenarios where $\alpha$ is small, a regime in which traditional slow-roll calculations often demand extensive computational resources.

This paper presents a parametric family of quasi-Fuchsian structures on the 3-punctured sphere that exhibit a distinct property: their evaluated foliations at infinity are identical to those of the corresponding Fuchsian structure. This achievement extends previous research by the same author [C. Camacho, J. Geom. Phys. 150 (2020) 103903], which established such an evaluation for punctured spheres with only one puncture.

This study investigates the dispersion of instantaneous yields within arbitrage-free pricing frameworks. The initial section establishes the correspondence between the instantaneous yield dispersion of any payoff and that of its dynamic hedging replicating strategy. It further demonstrates that the dispersion of the instantaneous yields of the dynamic hedging replicating strategy matches that of the dynamic hedging super-hedging strategy. The second section explores the implications of this result by analyzing the conditions under which the instantaneous yields dispersion of the dynamic hedging replicating strategy vanishes, concluding with an examination of the relationship between the dynamic hedging super-hedging strategy and the dynamic hedging replicating strategy.

Accurate diagnosis of cardiovascular diseases relies heavily on analyzing heart sounds, where modern research increasingly favors deep learning over traditional methods. However, this domain is hindered by a scarcity of high-quality, labeled datasets. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a heart sound categorization framework designed to function effectively even when trained on data corrupted with varying degrees of artificial noise. The proposed system employs two main components: first, an additive noise module that superimposes interference signals onto clean recordings to simulate real-world conditions; second, a deformation network that utilizes convolved upsampling steps to denoise the corrupted inputs. This architecture offers distinct advantages by operating with fewer trainable parameters and maintaining higher resilience to noise than standard autoencoders. Experimental results demonstrate that using 1-second heart sound segments, the framework successfully reduces error rates from a baseline of 14.1% (on noisy data) down to 4.8%, achieving performance comparable to that seen on clean datasets.

"In the attached letter, we established stringent upper bounds on a specific class of left-handed $Z$ boson couplings to up- and down-type quarks by analyzing cold atomic parity violation in $^{133}$Cs. Our methodology relies on perturbation theory to connect the $Z$-quark interaction strengths with modifications in the $^{133}$Cs electronic parity-violating amplitude, utilizing high-precision relativistic quantum chemical calculations to determine the necessary correlation factors. These hyperfine-independent constraints significantly surpass previous limits derived solely from electron-paradidron scattering analyses. The present work serves merely as a commentary; all arguments, mathematical derivations, and conclusions regarding this specific topic are fully elaborated in our primary publication referenced above."

This study investigates twists of torus-equivariant homotopy theory classified by $K(\mathbb{Z},3)$, specifically examining their behavior within the Borel construction for finite $G$-spectrum where $G$ is the 2-dimensional torus. The primary finding provides the unborl localization of $E\mathcal{L}_+^hC_E^S(G)$ for every finite $G$-spectrum $X$, where $\mathcal{L}_E$ denotes the Burnside category associated with the standard action of $G$ on $S^2$. The article further explores how these twists act upon equivariant stable homotopy classes from $X$ to $Y$, analyzing this action particularly for free $G$-spectra. As a derived consequence, the equitable twist of torus-equivariant cohomology theories on $S^n$ is characterized.

This study examines how social structures influence climate change, drawing on the S-shaped curve of societal development alongside the sigmoidal patterns of climate escalation. The proposed framework posits that societies progress through three distinct phases: initial growth, an intermediate transition, and final maturity. We analyze these stages and the critical threshold separating initial growth from final maturity, during which decisive action is required to prevent runaway warming. The intermediate phase is characterized by heightened uncertainty and risk, a period in which strategic decisions must be implemented to ensure a stable long-term future.

In this study, we examine boundedness properties of fractional $H^p$ spaces and further operators within the context of weighted ℓ^p spaces.

This study investigates how users respond to second-price auctions when auctions are conducted by untrustworthy vendors who falsely claim lower bids from some participants. Through a series of tasks, we found that awareness of deceptive practices does not deter bidding behavior, though perceived trust levels decline among bidding individuals. Additionally, we observed that deceptions have minimal impact on the auctions themselves, as they do not materially alter bidding strategies or auction outcomes.

We investigate the evolution of a four-dimensional, rotationally locally anisotropic symmetric (LRS) Bianchi-I spacetime within a $f(Q)$-gravitational framework. By integrating the Einstein field equations with the Raychaudhuri and shear expansion equations, we derive specific forms of the $f(Q)$ gravitational Lagrangian capable of yielding exact solutions to the field equations. These functional forms of $f(Q)$ successfully describe the behavior of the scale factor and shear tensor, demonstrating that the shear vanishes as $\lim_{\text{shear}} = 0$. This confirms an isotropic universe in the asymptotic limit, where $\lim_{\text{isotropy}} = \infty$. Furthermore, we analyze critical physical and kinematic characteristics of this cosmological model.

Hessenberg varieties, representing a specific class of algebraic varieties within the full flag manifold, serve as a fundamental object of study in algebraic geometry and have significant implications for combinatorics and invariant theory. This paper introduces a technique to parametrize regular nilpotent Hessenberg varieties using geometric vertex partitions, a method that generalizes both the Griffiths-Kessel formula and Borel's partial flag decomposition. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the combinatorics underlying these vertex partitions align precisely with the initial stages of Gr\"obner basis computations for Lie algebra nilpotent varieties, a process driven by the action of a torus.

Neural networks have become a prominent force in artistic creation, generating works ranging from music and paintings to movies and scripts. This article examines the underlying mechanisms of these AI systems, their integration into the broader art ecosystem, and their potential future trajectories.

The LHCb collaboration's recent measurements of neutral $B$ meson decays, which exhibit CP violation inconsistent with the Standard Model, are potentially explained by compositeness effects. We propose a specific framework where quarks interact with new composite resonances at an energy scale of approximately 10 TeV. This model simultaneously addresses the observed anomalies in kaon ($K$) and $B$ meson mixing while remaining consistent with existing constraints on the proton stability.

Knowledge-seeking Question Answering (Knowledge-Seeking QA) involves formulating queries to a system to acquire new information for problem-solving. Unlike standard QA systems that rely on a fixed knowledge base for questions and answers, interactions in Knowledge-Seeking QA are unconstrained by such a pre-defined corpus. This study introduces an extensive collection of knowledge-seeking queries constructed from research articles, accompanied by a companion companion service capable of responding to these inquiries. This companion, named ArticleAssistant, utilizes a large language model to generate answers by analyzing a repository of academic literature. Evaluated against a human-annotated dataset comprising 1,000 queries, the system achieved a human similarity score of 0.82 and a human precision score of 0.83.

We conducted three-dimensional core-collapse supernova simulations incorporating rapid neutrino-driven instabilities, utilizing a new feature of these phenomena where fluid vortex structures form in the presence of strong magnetic fields. These vortices generate significant entropy fluctuations that, in turn, amplify magnetic flux tubes through magnetic flux freezing. This positive feedback loop results in the rapid growth of these structures, causing magnetic fields to amplify by orders of magnitude within a few hundred microseconds. This amplification suppresses the original instability, leading to the disappearance of large-scale magnetic loops and the emergence of smaller-scale magnetic flux tubes. Crucially, this cycle creates a self-regulating mechanism that maintains magnetic field strength at levels sufficient to influence supernova dynamics while preventing field amplification from becoming excessively dominant.

Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a prevalent childhood condition characterized by inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. Although current diagnostic methods rely on subjective behavioral observations, they often result in inaccuracies and a lack of objectivity. This study introduces a novel deep learning framework designed to diagnose ADHD using resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) data. The framework begins by identifying crucial brain regions through a gradient-based approach that reduces dimensionality, subsequently feeding this selected data into a convolutional neural network (CNN) for diagnosis. The framework's efficacy was validated using the publicly available NIMH dataset, which comprised 108 rs-fMRI scans from children with ADHD and 108 scans from typically developing peers. The proposed method achieved an accuracy of 82.1%, a sensitivity of 81.5%, and a specificity of 82.7%. These results surpass those of existing state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating that focusing on key brain regions enhances the CNN's diagnostic performance.

We introduce a distinct-time epidemic SISI model, where continuous time is discretized into discrete steps. In this framework, a susceptible individual transitions to an infectious state at the subsequent time step with a fixed probability $p$. Furthermore, an infectious individual recovers or removes themselves from circulation (in a time-localized manner) at rate $1-p$. Consequently, the infection propagates across neighboring sites over adjacent discrete time transitions. We derive the exact critical threshold for the existence of an endemic state and map out the phase diagram by examining the system's long-term behavior. Additionally, we identify a second-order phase transition at a first-order jump in infected population density, termed "critical percolation by proxy." By analyzing system shortness, we present a method to estimate an accurate value for $\lambda_c$, achieving precision within $O(1/L)$.

Acronyms are ubiquitous in technical documentation, yet they frequently confuse non-native speakers and individuals outside the original technical community. To address this, we introduce MadDog, a web platform dedicated to acronym recognition and explanation. The system leverages a high-performance recognizer built on an acyclic directed mixed graph framework that models both phonetic and semantic relationships. To further enhance performance, a high-precision disambiguation mechanism was integrated. The accompanying dataset and comprehensive evaluation demonstrate that the system achieves an F1 score of 0.9155. Additionally, we discuss the data collection methodology and the overall system architecture in this paper.

This study introduces an innovative, compact architecture for efficient and adaptable control of electronic and thermal currents within quantum Hall (QH) systems. Current experiments reveal a switching mechanism where a periodic gate voltage generates either a unidirectional or bidirectional flow of charge and energy across a QH nano-device. This behavior stems from the interference of electron and phonon wavefunctions, governed by the dynamic geometry of the interferometer formed by quantum Hall edge states. Notably, when operating in thermal mode, this setup enables unidirectional heat transport and functions as a controllable heat diode, arising from frequency-dependent conductance governed by interference effects. The proposed design offers a straightforward pathway to engineer precise control over both energy and matter flows in diverse physical systems.

Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) storage has emerged as a promising technology for long-term archival solutions. However, real-world deployment faces challenges, including sequencing errors and inefficient retrieval mechanisms. This paper introduces a novel, highly effective protocol designed to concurrently manage updates to pointers and DNA sequences while simultaneously establishing and maintaining a B+-tree index structure. By leveraging the inherent self-assembly properties of DNA molecules, the proposed method achieves these objectives without incurring a single primer during the in-vitro storage retrieval process. Furthermore, by optimizing both molecular hierarchy and sequence-level data, the protocol enhances storage access efficiency.

Topological insulators, defined by protected nodal surfaces within momentum space, have recently attracted significant attention. This study offers a comprehensive examination of these momentum-space topological features, covering various types of nodal surfaces, their corresponding invariants, physical consequences, and experimental realizations. Particular emphasis is placed on photonic implementations, detailing the measurement of invariants via the parallel transport method and their related phenomena. The discussion further explores additional systems, including cold atoms, circuits, and materials, alongside an overview of promising avenues for future investigation.

Within tissues capable of excitation, propagating waves emerge from the synchronized activity of local elements, where this synchronization dictates wave speed. We establish an analytical framework to model the pacemaker, which induces traveling waves, and employ this framework to derive an estimation for wave velocity. The derived formula relies on the inherent properties of the excitable medium and the local dynamics of the wave source. Furthermore, we validate this theoretical estimation through simulations of cellular automata, and our findings align well with previous numerical estimates presented in literature.

This document outlines the storage duration for AI-related technical data, including logs, metrics, and model artifacts, alongside its associated retention policies. It also examines the strategies for deploying these workloads in the cloud, with specific focus on Azure containers, Kubernetes, and related cloud infrastructure. Additionally, the paper reviews AI operational flow, covering the end-to-end spectrum from data collection and preparation to model training, assessment, and deployment.

This study addresses ICD coding using a semi-supervised semi-markov approach, which was tested on the ICD-9/10 bridge dataset. The results demonstrate that this methodology significantly outperforms the original approach described in its primary source.

Cohen-Macaulay (CM) rings and CM-free modules are well-established notions within commutative algebra and algebraic combinatorics. In contrast, the concept of nearly Cohen-Macaulay (nearly CM) rings, which first emerged in the 1980s, has recently attracted significant interest. This note begins by defining nearly CM monomial ideals. Subsequently, we examine their properties, derive conditions for polymatroidal ideals to be nearly CM, and provide several illustrative examples to support these observations.

This paper introduces an unmonitored and monitored learning framework designed for class distributions that may be unmonitored or monitored but lack labeled samples. The proposed algorithm utilizes the quantum variational de-Heisenberg-Schreier transformation, which requires only a quantum circuit capable of executing a H\"{a}s to perform supervised or unsupervised classification. This method achieves quantum speedups for both monitored and unmonitored scenarios, outperforming existing approaches. The algorithm is demonstrated using a superconducting quantum processor, where it successfully learns distributions from real-world datasets such as MNIST and CIFAR-10. Results indicate that the proposed technique requires fewer measurements than current methods, while the monitored variant can be implemented using shallower circuits compared to its fully unmonitored version when applied to these datasets.

We present findings from a systematic investigation of the sky-wide KMTNet microlensing survey, utilizing an extensive sample of 2,012 events detected in the 2018 observing season across three bands (U, g, and r). These events were identified by applying a rigorous selection process to the original data, which filtered out known variables such as AGNs, RR Lyrae stars, and Cepheids, as well as other variable sources. The resulting dataset comprises 2,012 likely microlensing candidates, with 1,966 of them featuring complete light curves spanning all three observed bands. The sample spans events with Einstein radii ranging from 2.0 to 10.4 R$_{\odot}$ and lens masses between 0.0001 and 0.3 M$_{\odot}$. The majority of the lenses are stellar objects, specifically K and G type stars (K–G), while the event durations range from 1.3 to 30.3 days. The study also examines the spatial and temporal distributions of these candidates, revealing a concentration in the galactic plane and toward the Galactic Center, with no significant temporal evolution observed. Furthermore, we identify a higher incidence of multi-band events near the zenith, suggesting that atmospheric extinction plays a critical role in the variability amplitudes. Finally, we assess the likelihood of these candidates being gravitational lensing events by calculating the solid angle coverage

This paper introduces a differentiable method for calculating shadow images in low-light conditions, designed to enhance inverse problem research. We derive an effective shadow formation model and develop two loss functions to ensure consistency between predicted shadows and those in reference images. Additionally, we formulated two noise propagation equations to differentiate our shadow metrics. Integrating these elements yields a fully differentiable framework for shadow generation that avoids external dependencies. We employed this approach as a prior within a deep learning architecture to resolve phase retrieval, a task where no closed-form solution exists. Experiments on synthetic data demonstrate that our model achieves rapid and precise convergence, delivering competitive outcomes that rival those of established methods.

This study introduces a new statistical approach to origin-destination (OD) demand estimation, designed to minimize discrepancies between estimated and true OD matrices by leveraging daily traffic snapshots. The methodology is demonstrated using simulated data, and its robustness is validated through a real-world case study in the Barcelona metropolitan area.

Although extensive research has been conducted on the macroscopic behavior of oscillatory systems, a unified theoretical framework remains elusive. In this study, we utilize a unifying mathematical formalism to examine the equilibrium states of a broad class of oscillators. The resulting mathematical structure is uniform across various oscillators, consisting of a "small" phase-coupling system of differential equations situated on a high-dimensional torus. By placing general restrictions on this coupling system, we derive sufficient conditions for the existence of fully synchronized states. Furthermore, we explore the specific dynamics of arrays formed by diverse oscillators, demonstrating that their small phase-coupling equations often map to well-known large-scale models found in previous literature.

A uniform spanning tree represents a probability distribution over all possible ways to connect $n$ labeled vertices using exactly $n-1$ edges without forming any cycles. Two primary algorithms exist for constructing these trees: the Wilson algorithm, which relies on loop-erased random walks, and the Aldous-Broder method, which captures the first visit of a random walk to each new vertex. This study demonstrates that the Aldous-Broder method can be integrated with a modified version of Wilson's algorithm to achieve a two-phase framework. The initial phase involves a random walk that continues until $n$ distinct vertices are visited; during the subsequent phase, these visits are processed to remove any generated loops. This hybrid approach offers a generalized perspective on tree generation, and in the degenerate case where the walk is completed after visiting all vertices in phase 1, it effectively replicates the standard Wilson algorithm.

Sheet music serves as a universal language for musical audio, yet current methods for converting between these two formats are constrained by the need for parallel, human-annotated scores. To address this limitation, we introduce the **MusicTM-Dataset**, a resource of 10,000 sheet music files paired with corresponding musical audio and textual lyrics, but lacking direct audio-score transcriptions. This large-scale collection enables a unified representation learning framework that learns to map sheet music and lyrics into a shared latent space, effectively aligning generated audio with visual scores. We evaluated various models, including those based on variational autoencoders (VAEs), and our proposed **MusicTM-VAE** achieved a high reconstruction accuracy of 0.886 on the Mel-64 space, surpassing all baselines. This model supports three primary applications: (1) creating sheet music from audio, (2) transcribing sheet music based on lyrics provided during audio playback, and (3) synchronizing lyric display with the sheet music during listening.

This study explores how pre-trained embedding models, such as Word2Vec, GloVe, and FastText, can be applied to analyze ontologies representing encyclopedic knowledge. By mapping ontology class names to vector spaces, this approach enables the investigation of inter-class relationships through techniques inspired by natural language processing. The research utilizes Ontodia and Python's `pywikibot` library to access structural and wiki text data via the Wikidata API, thereby deriving class embeddings and calculating derived metrics. These metrics include centroid-based similarity, Fran\c{c}ket-Ben\c{c}houit (FB) similarity, and Lin similarity. The resulting metrics are analyzed and contrasted against traditional methods like Euler and probabilistic similarities to offer a deeper understanding of the visual data examination process.

The presence of an intensity-dependent (ID) dispersion coefficient is a characteristic feature of diverse nonlinear systems. This work examines the nonlinear Schr\"odinger (LSE) equation governing self-stealing pulses, which depend on such intensity-dependent dispersion. By applying a perturbation approach relative to dark solitons in the limit of low background intensity, we demonstrate that stability is maintained up to third-order perturbative corrections. Furthermore, numerical investigations into dark soliton perturbations up to non-perturbative third-order levels confirm stability, with only minor shifts in both amplitude and position observed.

Interpreting extensive and intricate real-world datasets demands human support, necessitating visual analytics systems that bridge the gap between limited cognitive and attentional capacities and analytical requirements. Effectively designing such systems is a complex undertaking involving multiple stakeholders, including domain experts, usability specialists, and visual designers, who must collaborate to ensure the final tools are both functional and intuitive. This paper introduces "Lotse," a novel framework for orchestrating user assistance within visual analytics. It outlines both a theoretical model for the design process and a prototype system. Furthermore, the authors examine an early prototype applied to a specific data analysis task to demonstrate its capabilities and validate its application.

Optimizing the configuration of modular helical or toroidal coil systems is an essential step in designing compact fusion reactors, a task that can be achieved using high-dimensional optimization techniques. These methods address a broad objective function that evaluates critical factors, including single-null divertor positioning, magnetic well depth, and the alignment of poloidal flux contours. Once a base configuration is identified, additional coils are often required to correct for residual neoclassical transport or structural limitations. Consequently, our objective is to streamline the multi-objective optimization of these enhancement coils. We demonstrate that our approach successfully generates stellarators featuring enhanced stability and improved stability, specifically by adding coils to existing configurations.

A non-invasive experimental technique utilizing magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to map temperature-induced changes in proton spin density within a gas-solid bed is presented. Specifically, a fast MRI protocol was implemented to acquire images of a bed of 1.5 mm plastic spheres as carbon dioxide flowed through it. Subsequently, these images were corrected for relaxation effects to generate images of gas-solid interaction zones. By combining these structural images with quantitative $T_1$ relaxation times and Nusselt number calculations, the study establishes a new framework for quantifying heat transfer in moving fluid-solid systems. This approach demonstrates that the MRI method can accurately capture temperature distributions in fluidized beds, even when the thermal contrast between phases is low.

This study investigates the self-organization of self-assembling biomolecular units that form aggregates with a fixed stoichiometry of $N$ components, where each component type possesses its own interaction matrix. Initially, the system's behavior in the incompressible limit is explored; under these conditions, the order parameter dynamics adhere to the Cahn-Hilliard equation with non-constant coefficients, while energy evolution is governed by a partial differential equation (PDE) involving interaction matrices for both energy and dissipation that are periodic. A key finding is the emergence of spatially heterogeneous steady states in the order parameter, driven by the interplay between individual tendency toward specific wavelength selection and system-wide conservation laws. Consequently, global aggregate composition results from a negotiation among local preferences and conservation constraints, a process that yields a final state dependent on multiple factors, including the specific spatial arrangement of preference length scales. Furthermore, in a numerical simulation of a two-component system, a mechanism is identified where biomolecules exhibiting mutual attraction segregate into domains, with the number of such domains dictated by the balance of local conservation rules and local preferential scales.

This study examines the evolution of sunspot groups and magnetic disturbances during solar eruptions, utilizing observations from the Solar Dynamics Observatory's Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA) and Magnetograph (MAG). The analysis focuses on Active Region (AR) 11429, a large complex located near the solar disk center during the peak of Solar Cycle 25. The study identifies three distinct sub-rotations within this region, labeled Group A, Group B, and Group C. While Group A and Group B are defined by their respective sunspot maximums, Group C is characterized by a binary sunspot maximum. The investigation details the emergence, growth, peak, and decay phases of these groups, as well as the sunspot numbers and sunspot indices for each. Additionally, the paper analyzes the timing and characteristics of coronal mass ejections (CMEs) and X-class solar flares. The results indicate that Group A and Group B experienced a total of 3 CMEs and 2 X-class flares, whereas Group C produced 2 CMEs and 1 X-class flare. Principles and conjectures that were once deemed fragile have occasionally been resolved through the discovery of profound new theorems; a notable instance is the proof of the Lang conjecture, which established the strong Mason–Gröbner (principle). This paper explores further examples, beginning with an analysis of the weak Mason–Gröbner principle and its potential future robustification to the `b`-principle. We demonstrate that Greenberg's conjecture concerning the `b`-principle follows directly from the Taniyama–Shimura–Wiles theorem. Additionally, we outline connections between the `b`-principle and various problems in arithmetic geometry, including those addressed by Serre's Conjecture, Deligne's conjecture, and hypotheses regarding Beilinson regulators.

Accurate predictions of cardiac mechanics rely on robust numerical methods, specifically the use of multilevel preconditioners to accelerate convergence during finite element simulations. This study evaluates several scalable multilevel preconditioners for cardiac mechanics by comparing their performance against each other and against standard unpreconditioned approaches. The analysis focuses on key metrics including condition number reduction, system solve times, total simulation time, and solution accuracy. The findings indicate that scalable multilevel methods are essential for efficient cardiac simulations, demonstrating that both computation accuracy and total efficiency depend critically on the specific type of multilevel strategy employed.

Social tagging systems enable users to collaboratively annotate web resources, yet their full potential remains largely untapped. This study investigates four key dimensions: reuse, interest exchange, user collaboration, and user interest evolution. We analyze collaborative behavior by examining tag and resource data from del.icio.us and quantifying individual user collaboration through their tag-sharing activities. Additionally, we assess interest exchange by measuring the overlap of resources bookmarked by user pairs and explore the temporal dynamics of user interest by analyzing fluctuations in their focused topics and resource types over time. Our findings indicate that while collaborative behavior is prevalent, its impact on interest exchange and temporal interest dynamics is minimal.

This work demonstrates the fabrication of functional acoustic metagratings operating at ultrahigh frequencies (1–10 GHz), corresponding to wavelengths between 300 µm and 30 µm. These devices were created using two-photon polymerization, a technique capable of producing microstructures with sub-wavelength precision. The resulting metagrating features a periodic arrangement of cylindrical pillars with diameters ranging from 10 to 50 µm. Experimental results show that these structures function as effective beam deflectors, achieving maximum deflection efficiencies of 60% at 1.25 GHz and 40% at 5 GHz. Numerical simulations align closely with experimental measurements, and the study provides general guidelines for designing microacoustic devices with patterned surfaces.

This work examines the long-term dynamics of the two-dimensional robust FENE dumbbell model for compressible Oldroyd 1/-fluids, which accounts for finite extensibility of the dumbbells. First, it is demonstrated that the global robust solution exhibits uniform-in-time boundedness within a certain range; consequently, the $\omega$-limit set of the solution is proven to be compact and invariant. Second, under the assumption of small initial data in the $H^2\times H^1$ norm, it is established that the solution decays exponentially toward the constant state $( ar{ho}, ar{Y}) = (1,1)$, where the result relies on the $\omega$-limit set being solution-independent. Lastly, for the scenario involving large initial data, the article derives the precise asymptotic asymptotic decay rates of the global robust solution.

The evolution of 5G wireless networks demands a shift from centralized to highly distributed architectures to meet the stringent requirements of emerging services. A viable solution for this decentralization is the Non-Backhaul (NB) model, which enables infrastructure sharing among network operators through devices functioning as both base stations and user equipment. This article examines the challenges inherent in Non-Backhaul (IAB), outlines potential remedies, and reviews current research to identify key obstacles that must be addressed to advance the field. Finally, it proposes a roadmap for future investigations aimed at advancing IAB technology.

The hyperparameter tuning process is essential for optimizing the performance of many machine learning algorithms, including those used for ranking. Traditional approaches, such as grid search, are often impractical due to the excessive computational costs they incur. This paper introduces a methodology for evaluating the influence of hyperparameters on the performance of the pbest evolutionary algorithm (EA) for the bi-criteria ranking problem. We employ the Sobol' sensitivity analysis method to assess how global hyperparameter interactions affect performance, specifically measuring their individual contributions to the final solution's efficiency and the rate of convergence. Our analysis reveals that the pbest parameter exerts the most significant impact on both efficiency and convergence, followed by the selection mechanism, mutation probability, and genetic crossover likelihood. We also note a considerable interaction effect between pbest and the selection mechanism. These empirical findings are intended to guide practitioners in more effectively configuring their evolutionary algorithm parameters.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has proven effective for addressing diverse decision-making challenges, yet the rapid proliferation of novel RL agents has created a pressing need for a comprehensive ecosystem to test new methods. We introduce L2Explorer, a newly established, open-source RL evaluation ecosystem designed to address this gap. As an ever-expanding collection of over 200 benchmarks, it enables rapid prototyping and validation of innovative agents. Furthermore, we integrate a sophisticated difficulty estimation technique to categorize these tasks into distinct difficulty levels. Beyond the benchmarks, L2Explorer hosts over 100 established agent implementations, including industry-standard baselines, to facilitate direct performance comparisons. We also engineered a unified, user-friendly API that standardizes agent registration and benchmark evaluation, streamlining the contribution process for the community. To demonstrate the platform's utility, we conducted a large-scale experiment evaluating over 1,000 agents across our benchmarks, identifying previously unknown solutions for specific tasks. L2Explorer is open to contributions and can be accessed at https://github.com/iiic-ai-lab/L2Explorer.

Liger is a collaborative initiative at Keck Observatory designed to integrate and analyze data from the two Keck telescopes, which operate with distinct instruments and control systems. As an essential component of this project, the data acquisition system (KPS-DAS) manages the flow of raw data from the hardware to KPS-COR, a core function detailed in the paper's introduction. This system accommodates inputs from four imaging detectors and two spectrograph cameras, handling both data packaging and the management of source identifiers. KPS-DAS processes these streams by multiplexing them into a unified output for the KPS-COR application. Furthermore, the paper outlines the software architecture and implementation specifics, emphasizing the system's flexibility to facilitate future data source integrations.

This work establishes the existence of a family of traveling wave solutions to the 2D Navier-Stokes equation, situated between two Couette flows characterized by differing velocities. The identified solution is unique up to a Galilean transformation and is a smooth perturbation of one Couette flow decaying exponentially toward the second Couette flow. This solution arises from a bifurcation occurring at a critical Reynolds number; however, because of nonlinearity, this bifurcation is not branching but rather supercritical. The results rely on a combination of spectral analysis, an a priori estimate, and Fredholm theory.

In excition-polariton condensates, the all-optical manipulation of linear polarization is achieved by balancing the lengths of two parallel pathways. This study presents an analytical framework for a system where these pathways interact, revealing that the standard mean-field theory is insufficient for fully describing the resulting nonlinear current. We offer both a theoretical model and experimental verification of this framework, demonstrating its strong agreement with observed phenomena. Furthermore, we demonstrate the stable generation of tunable all-optically controlled linear polarization using the condensate.

We introduce a class of deterministic, Burgers- and KPZ-type equations characterized by a nonlocal second-order derivative. Formulated as gradient flows within a suitable metric space, these dynamical systems generate self-similar singular solutions that enable the derivation of a coherent, large-scale statistical description of interfaces. This macroscopic framework is benchmarked against the well-established Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) equation results. The analysis relies on rigorous mathematical foundations, specifically the theory of Young measures and Young integration.

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread illness and death globally, prompting governments worldwide to implement measures aimed at slowing viral transmission. Effective policy decisions require a thorough understanding of the epidemic's progression, a goal hindered in many regions by inadequate data collection and infrastructure. This paper examines the challenges South Africa encountered while gathering epidemic data and analyzes the specific impacts those hurdles had on the efficacy of its containment strategies.

Glaucoma and Diabetic Retinopathy are prevalent retinal disorders that, if detected early, are manageable; however, their late-stage progression often leads to blindness. This study focuses on automating the categorization of these conditions by fusing multimodal data, specifically combining the strengths of two distinct deep learning architectures: one trained on clinical reports and another on retinal images. By integrating image and textual data, the proposed method enhances diagnostic accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate that this fused approach surpasses models using a single modality, achieving a test accuracy of 94.3%.

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread illness and death globally, with chest X-rays emerging as a primary diagnostic tool for identifying infected individuals. While current research confirms that COVID-19 exhibits radiological features similar to pneumonia, the specific nature of the disease's unique X-ray characteristics remains uncertain. This study aims to explore the potential traits of COVID-19 ICU admissions by analyzing X-ray image data.

Transmission eigenfunctions are defined as solutions to Helmholtz equations within both the interior and exterior of a scatterer, sharing identical Helmholtz data on the boundary, with their internal wavenumbers exceeding the exterior wavenumbers. Unlike previous research limited to homogeneous spheres, this study investigates the identification of these eigenfunctions in targets with spherical layered structures. We establish a solvable boundary value problem on the eigenfunctions themselves and demonstrate that their spherical harmonic degrees can be uniquely determined from measurements taken solely within the annular region. Notably, this determination requires data from any single spherical surface and involves just one radial field measurement.

Identifying user intent is a critical component of natural language processing (NLP) systems, particularly within the intent identification (II) task. While existing approaches predominantly rely on large-scale datasets, the scarcity of such resources for specific II subtasks limits the generalization capabilities of current models. This paper presents a novel II framework that utilizes pre-training and comparative learning to enhance generalization. The framework consists of two stages: (1) a pre-training phase employing contrastive autoencoders to capture inter-class correlations, followed by (2) an unsupervised comparison step that trains classifiers by contrasting similar and dissimilar input samples. Experimental results across three II datasets demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses state-of-the-art baselines, specifically showing significant improvements on the challenging e-commerce dataset.

In the context of simplicial homotopy theory, the simplicial set representing the mapping space between two objects $\mathbf{Q}$ and $\mathbf{P}$ in a model category serves as the fundamental building block. This paper demonstrates that within a convenient adequate Quatuern structure, the space of simplicial bundles over a fixed base $\mathbf{B}$—defined as the fibrations over $\mathbf{B}$ with fixed fiber $\mathbf{F}$ at the terminal object of this space—is equivalent to the space of minimal fibrations. This specific equivalence constitutes a cofibrant approximation of the mapping space between $\mathbf{Q}$ and $\mathbf{P}$. The study also establishes that the subcategory consisting of fibrations with fibers weakly equivalent to a fixed simplicial set $\mathbf{F}$ forms a convenient adequate Quatuern structure.

Detecting visual associations within images is a fundamental challenge in computer vision. While numerous studies have addressed this, most rely on supervised methods that generate a vast number of false positives, particularly for infrequent concepts. This study introduces a novel, fully unsupervised framework designed to enhance detection accuracy by eliminating these false positives. Initially, the visual association detector processes the entire dataset, generating both valid detections and errors. Subsequently, a clustering process groups similar concepts, and for each resulting cluster, we propose an unsupervised metric to filter out cluster-specific false positives. Finally, this method was validated across three datasets, yielding encouraging results that demonstrate its viability and potential for future applications.

The cost associated with weakly measuring a quantum system is analyzed. It is demonstrated that conducting such measurements on $N$ times is equivalent to performing a strongly repeated $N$ times, which degrades the remaining coherence by a factor of $N$. This finding is supported by calculations within two specific models: first, by examining how strongly decoherence degrades after strong measurement in an ideal qubit system, and second, by analyzing the measurement of a photon's polarization using another photon as the probe.

Social networks are increasingly vital for analyzing social behaviors and relationships. While existing research has developed various models to extract these graphs from unstructured text, no single framework currently exists to handle this task comprehensively. To address this gap, we propose **SRGNet**, an innovative end-to-end neural architecture designed to extract edges for social relationship construction. SRGNet utilizes three core components: a Document Encoder to encode text, an Edge Scoring mechanism to evaluate the social relationship between any word pair, and a Global Aggregation module to encode document-level context. We further refined the model using advanced techniques, including self-attention mechanisms, dropout, and batch normalization. Evaluated against three publicly available datasets, SRGNet demonstrated superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art models.

To address visual identification tasks, including object and scene recognition, this paper introduces a new framework utilizing deep graph convolutional networks (DCGNNs). This system is designed to capture and replicate the inductive reasoning capabilities of human vision by modeling the explicit and implicit spatial-temporal relationships among entities in visual data as a dynamic graph. We propose a novel DCGNN-driven framework, named Dynamic Graph Message Transmission Network (DGMSNet), which facilitates efficient information flow across both intra- and inter-graph structures. Specifically, the network employs an Entity-level Dynamic Graph Transmission (EDGT) module to disseminate node data within a single frame, alongside a Frame-level Dynamic Graph Transmission (FDGT) module that conveys graph-level features sequentially over time. This dual mechanism enables DGMSNet to perform node- and graph-level feature extraction for identification purposes, effectively modeling the complex spatial-temporal dependencies among entities. Experiments on four object recognition benchmarks and two visual identification tasks for scene analysis demonstrate that DGMSNet achieves state-of-the-art performance. Furthermore, a comprehensive ablation study provides deep insights into the model's functional characteristics and confirms the critical role of the proposed dual transmission mechanisms.

This study introduces a novel hardware architecture for multi-constant integer multiplication, designed to handle any set of predetermined constants. The proposed system employs a minimal hardware footprint by utilizing the smallest possible count of 256-based adders and 256-based multipliers, alongside a fresh algorithm that efficiently computes the associated coefficients for these constants. Furthermore, an original methodology for determining the bit-width of each generated coefficient is detailed. The second part of the paper presents an enhanced algorithm to generate a hardware graph representing the numerous multi-constant multiplication process, which surpasses the results of established state-of-the-art algorithms. The third part outlines a novel algorithm for constructing a linear array graph derived from this structure, yielding linear array configurations that outperform results from current leading methods. The final section evaluates both integer and floating-point implementations using both synthetic and real-world data sets. The results highlight a significant performance gain, demonstrating that the new system is substantially more efficient than existing state-of-the-art solutions.

This paper explores Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs), detailing their fundamental principles and applications. We outline the distinctions between classical and quantum neural architectures, emphasizing how quantum-specific features like entanglement and interference are leveraged within these models. Several current and emerging application areas are introduced, alongside an analysis of the inherent challenges that limit widespread adoption of QNNs in industry. The conclusion provides a brief outlook on potential future research paths.

The RF Booster R&D activities for the Snowmass 2021 process were organized within the Accelerator Components and Systems R&D Working Group (WG-A7), which was further divided into three specialized subgroups. These subgroups addressed critical aspects of the system, including the development of RF Booster architectures, the design of high-power cavities, and the advancement of high-performance electronic components. This document encapsulates the findings and discussions from those dialogues.

The LHC's discovery of the Higgs boson concluded its primary mission, yet addressing unresolved physics questions demands a more potent colliding system. Since the Large Hadron Collider (SH) is not suitable for this next phase, alternative facilities are required. The muon collider stands out as a compelling choice for a complementary machine, offering superior capabilities to clarify various phenomena beyond the reach of the SH. This paper outlines the various project initiatives and development milestones regarding the muon collider while also examining the significant technical hurdles—specifically rapid demagnetization issues—associated with muon beams.

We examine how linear perturbations travel through a viscous relativistic fluid in equilibrium, considering both shear and bulk viscosity coefficients. Our analysis reveals that propagation is only causal and stable if a specific, newly derived inequality involving the energy density, viscous viscosities, and speed of light is satisfied. This inequality must be satisfied by a quark-gluon plasma to be consistent with recent relativistic hydrodynamic simulations of heavy-ion collision experiments.

Recent findings from the LIGO-Virgo collaboration regarding gravitational waves from merging primordial black holes (PBHs) have prompted a re-examination of the potential cosmic background of radio waves emitted by these events. This study investigates the radio particle emission arising from accretion around PBHs within the redshift interval $0.01 < z < 10$. We model the radio signal generated by electrons in the intergalactic medium being captured by PBHs and accreted, which subsequently radiate via synchrotron mechanisms within the magnetosphere. Our analysis indicates that, for a universal density fraction of $\Omega_{\rm PBH}/\Omega_{\rm crit} \sim 10^{-2}$, the cumulative radio power from this process could reach $10^{43}$ erg s$^{-1}$. This level is sufficient to account for the observed flux of the radio point source J0437$-$4715, a phenomenon potentially explainable by the radio emission of a single, recent PBH merger occurring at $z \sim 0.01$.

Homomorphic encryption enables computations on ciphertexts that yield ciphertexts corresponding to the results of those operations. Although significant progress has been made in CPU-compatible HE, current state-of-the-art software libraries remain prohibitively slow for practical use. This paper introduces Virtual Safe, a processor architecture designed to accelerate HE operations. We identify three optimization strategies: (1) leveraging HE arithmetic properties to simplify gate logic, (2) employing a lookup table for data acceleration, and (3) implementing a five-stage pipeline. By applying these optimizations within a modular, pipelined processor running over the Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) library (lib) Tiny Functional Encryption (TFE), we achieve a performance speedup of 2.0 to 2 orders of magnitude compared to leading software implementations.

The weighted CSP problem involves minimizing a collection of constraints applied to variable assignments. In this work, we address the challenge of achieving a constant-factor approximation for constraints featuring an arbitrary number of variables and sparse instances. Our primary contribution is a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) that functions as a local search algorithm capable of improving upon the best current constant-factor results by Rastogi et al. (2019). This method improves solutions through localized perturbations of sparse configurations, a process supported by a counting argument that demonstrates the existence of superior neighboring instances. We further demonstrate the efficacy of this strategy by designing and analyzing enhanced sparse transformations that facilitate more effective local searches.

Pretrained language models (LMs) have become a cornerstone of natural language processing, enabling solutions to a wide variety of tasks. However, ensuring these models operate safely and reliably within production environments remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces FEAAL (Few-example Faithfulness Assessment), a method designed to evaluate how production-ready systems perform under few-shot conditions. Our approach measures two critical aspects: (1) the accuracy of a production model compared to a high-quality baseline, and (2) the consistency between a model's confidence and its actual performance. We demonstrate using the RoBERTa-base architecture that production models often exhibit higher error rates and lower confidence levels in few-shot scenarios compared to fine-tuned base-line models, and notably display a larger gap between confidence and accuracy. These findings suggest that existing confidence mechanisms may be unreliable in few-shot production settings, underscoring the urgent need for more robust evaluation techniques.

Although urban semantic segmentation has been extensively studied using visible-light imagery, it remains an under-explored domain within hyperspectral imagery (HSI). This paper introduces a weakly-supervised framework designed to generate high-precision semantic maps for cityscape HSI with only minimal supervision. The core methodology relies on an iterative, unsupervised clustering process that partitions HSI pixels into distinct semantic classes by harnessing both spectral and textural characteristics. To refine segmentation accuracy, we integrate a CRF-based post-processing step that leverages mid-level cues, such as edge information. Extensive experiments conducted on the cityscape dataset with four different spectral bands demonstrate that our approach yields superior performance compared to existing weakly-supervised cityscape segmentation methods.

The evolution of close-orbiting exoplanets is frequently explained by tidal dissipation within the host star drawing the planets toward a stellar merger. However, this mechanism struggles to account for ultra-short-period planets (those with periods under three days) because stellar tides become inefficient at moving planets across the planet-host distance in the day-to-ten-day range. Recent studies suggest that angular momentum transfer from stellar tides to the planet's spin offers a solution to this bottleneck. We investigate this hypothesis by analyzing the correlation between the g-mode frequencies of g-type stars and the orbital periods of their companions. We find that ultra-short-period planets are significantly more likely to orbit F-type stars possessing high-frequency g-modes, a link that weakens as planetary periods lengthen. This observation supports the idea that stellar spin-down facilitates the formation of ultra-short-period planets via angular momentum exchange. Furthermore, we estimate the efficiency of this process and discuss its implications for understanding angular momentum retention in systems hosting g-type stars.

However, a prior study established that the constant-time feasibility of these operations depends on the specific bit length.
