Blends arise when multiple independent observations are aggregated, a scenario prevalent in fields such as agriculture, mining, and manufacturing. This study introduces the generalized maximum likelihood (GML) approach to estimate the mean of these blended datasets. When the population distribution is Gaussian, GML yields an exact estimate; notably, if the blend components share a common variance, the GML value coincides with the traditional sample mean. A key advantage of GML is its extensibility to non-normal distributions, where it provides an asymptotically valid estimate. Furthermore, the GML framework generates asymptotic variance estimates and confidence intervals for this central tendency.

While established differential privacy (DP) definitions ensure privacy even when an adversary possesses side information, these guarantees can fail if side information extends beyond the query data itself to include attributes dependent on the query data known to the adversary. This paper provides a technical demonstration that one-sided privacy breaches occur in such scenarios where the side information is theoretically determined by the query data, specifically when relying on standard DP definitions. We introduce a framework quantifying the magnitude of these breaches through an extension of conditional differential privacy (CDP), offering both necessary and sufficient conditions to determine privacy breach levels caused by this dependency. Our proposed CDP metric effectively generalizes the original concept and enables precise characterization of privacy risks in these dependent, real-world cases.

The AS 209 protoplanetary disk is renowned for its prominent outer carbon monoxide (CO) gap, a feature that has generated considerable debate regarding the mechanisms driving it. This study utilizes ALMA observations to investigate the disk's structure and chemical composition, employing radiative transfer modeling to explore the physical and chemical environments. Our findings indicate that a CO gap exists within the disk, situated slightly closer to the central star than the CO emission boundary suggests. Furthermore, the midplane gas within the inner disk region is largely depleted of CO, with the exception of a narrow chemical layer immediately beneath the CO gap. This configuration is consistent with a scenario where dust grains undergo CO freeze-out, resulting in CO gas reduction. Alternatively, chemical transformation could explain these observations if dust grain accretion removes CO from the gas phase while simultaneously enriching carbon in the gas through CO destruction and conversion into methane (CH₄). These results suggest that both dust grain growth and chemical CO destruction are active processes within the disk. Consequently, the current data cannot definitively distinguish between the two, though further radiative transfer modeling combined with additional chemical observations are required to resolve the ambiguity.

In this paper, we introduce the R package "efftool," which offers an effective toolkit for analyzing timestamped data. This package enables researchers to conduct several related analyses, allowing them to evaluate the predictive capabilities of one variable based on another time series. Specifically, "efftool" facilitates: (1) calculating effective and lagged correlation matrices; (2) generating visualizations that support the interpretation of time series relationships; and (3) creating lagged graphical models. We demonstrate the package's functionality using the RStudio Interactive Bookshelves features and provide an intuitive interface for both users and developers.

In this paper, we address the control mean games associated with an average discount factor, specifically under constraints involving the state. By adapting the approach proposed by Delboeuf and Zhang, existence "gentle" solutions are demonstrated. Control in these contexts features vector elements, with state constraints defined through both inequality and equality conditions. The case concerning equalities is managed by incorporating supplementary control variables.

In this study, we investigate the spatial organization of young stellar populations within the galactic disk, utilizing the Gaia Data Release 2 (DR2) catalog. Our analysis focuses on the "threads" referenced in the 2018 Gaia DR2 release, which depict apparent linear groupings of stars near the galactic plane. By applying a clustering algorithm, we demonstrate that these observed "threads" are predominantly artifacts resulting from the superposition of stellar populations belonging to distinct spiral arms. We propose that these perceived linear structures are not unique to specific age cohorts but rather reflect the inherent spatial distribution of all Galactic disk populations, given the accuracy of current astrometric data. Furthermore, we introduce a novel methodology for quantifying the age-dependent large-scale distribution of Galactic disk objects, revealing that age-related variations are subtle and largely confined to the outer disk. In the inner regions, the spatial arrangement of these groups closely mirrors the apparent "threads," indicating a lack of significant structural divergence by age.

Visual inconsistency detection aims to flag pairs of items flagged as incompatible, such as mismatching apparel ensembles. Focusing on fashion data, we introduce VICTOR, a data-driven framework that pinpoints visual inconsistencies without relying on manually crafted rules. To achieve this, we employ a dual strategy: a fine-grained classifier powered by a Transformer-based vision encoder and a pre-training procedure utilizing domain-specific fashion contrasts. Our approach is evaluated against two standard datasets, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing methods, with evaluations extending to an industry-adjacent clothing product catalog.

Light asset theories provide a unified framework for understanding various forms of nonclassical light. In this paper, we offer a preliminary overview of the generalized nonclassical light asset theory proposed in reference [Phys. Rev. A 104, 013101 (2021)]. We introduce the light asset concept and demonstrate its robustness by showing that asset multiplication corresponds precisely to the well-established asset subtraction operation found in quantum optics. Furthermore, we introduce a $\mathcal{P}$-representable light asset theory for generalized nonclassical light, where the quasi-probability distribution is defined on the extended phase space.

This paper investigates the convergence properties of federated learning, a distributed training framework where a central server updates a global model based on gradients received from remote clients holding local datasets. Due to network latency and bandwidth constraints, these distant data sources cannot transmit gradient information to the server in a timely manner. We analyze an aggregation strategy we term Buffered Synchronous Aggregation (BSA), in which the server collects gradients from all $n$ clients within a time window of $2T$ seconds. Specifically, every $T$ seconds, the BSA synchronously merges the most recent gradient batch arriving from each of the $n$ clients. We demonstrate that for a sufficiently large synchronization interval $T$, the BSA acts as an anti-gradient for the global model, thereby decelerating its convergence. Consequently, we establish that both vanilla federated learning with BSA and BSA with privacy-preserving additive Gaussian mechanism noise impose lower bounds on the number of iterations required to achieve $\epsilon$-accuracy. These theoretical findings are verified through experiments on synthetic data and the MNIST benchmark.

This study defines a common framework within polynomial tempered function algebra to derive both operational formulas and resolvent operator representations. Specifically, we establish the conditions required for generating a one-parameter semigroup of continuous linear operators on $C_{\infty}^1$, a space consisting of continuously differentiable bounded continuous complex-valued functions on $\mathbb{R}$ equipped with the topology induced by uniform convergence. Furthermore, we demonstrate the construction of operational calculus relative to specific differential operators, namely $\frac{d}{dt}$ and the tensor product $\frac{d}{dt} \otimes d$.

This study investigates the fraction of the universe's total mass comprised of primordial black holes (PBHs) across various mass ranges. We demonstrate that even black holes with masses as low as 1000 kg would constitute a substantial portion of the cosmos, provided their abundance falls within current observational limits. To achieve this, we first derive an explicit formula for the density of matter within an individual PBH and subsequently integrate the standard constraints from cosmology to determine the allowable abundance for PBHs of any given mass. Finally, we calculate the total universal mass fraction attributed to the entire PBH population. Our findings indicate that the density of PBHs with masses situated between 10 and 1000 kg closely matches the calculated fraction required to explain dark matter.

This paper examines fractures within particle-based, two-dimensional layered structures known as atomically thin sheets or "atomic sheets" (AS). These fractures are governed by inter-particle forces, which we model using a simplified Hertzian framework. The study reveals that the geometry of the resulting cracks is highly sensitive to the magnitude of the normal compressive stress acting between layers. Specifically, we analyze how stresses concentrate around the tips of such tips, demonstrating that these concentrations scale with a power law of exponent 1/2 relative to the distance from the tip. We further present numerical results indicating that the ultimate strength of the sheet is governed by its largest flaw, analogous to the principles of Griffith fracture theory.

Lattice alignment strategies utilizing GaN with anisotropic wide-bandgap materials like $ZnGeN_2$ and $MgSiN_2$ have been investigated to induce strain-induced modifications in carrier transport. Employing first-principles calculations, we demonstrate that applying epitaxial compressive strain along the c-axis and tensile strain along the a-axis in GaN significantly enhances hole conductivity by approximately three orders of magnitude. Conversely, electron mobility is suppressed by this specific strain combination. In contrast, an epitaxial configuration subjecting GaN to overall compressive strain along both axes results in a substantial increase in electron mobility while simultaneously reducing hole mobility. These findings indicate that lattice-matching epitaxy can drastically modulate the carrier type and conductivity levels within $GaN$, offering potential for advanced electronic applications.

This study introduces a nonlinear regression approach designed to handle functionally significant tasks, specifically denoting them as Temporal Variation Learning (TVL). TVL is implemented using Sparse Gaussian Process (SGP) models, which partition a regression function into a time-invariant component and a time-dependent component. The former is shared by all functions within a dataset, whereas the latter evolves with time and is parameterized as a temporal function, the critical "temporal variation point" (TVP). By selecting only those time points where this evolution is most pronounced, TVL achieves significant model sparsification. A primary application of TVL lies in marine robot navigation, where it addresses position estimation amidst noisy sensor data. Furthermore, the proposed system supports active learning by determining the optimal locations for acquiring new data. Simulation results confirm that the proposed method yields superior learning efficiency and enhanced estimation accuracy.

A complex isothermal surface is defined as a conformal mapping $f: \Sigma \to \mathbb{C}P^1$ from a Riemann surface $\Sigma$ to the Riemann sphere, characterized by its associated data $(\lambda, \mu)$, where $\lambda$ represents the trace and $\mu$ the determinant of the associated linear ODE $u'' + (\lambda/2)u = 0$. Specifically, $\lambda$ and $\mu$ are meromorphic 1-forms of specific types. A primary finding of this work demonstrates that given any pair of meromorphic 1-forms $(\lambda, \mu)$, there exists an corresponding isothermal surface $f$, up to an automorphism of the domain $\Sigma$. Furthermore, we establish a one-to-one correspondence between the group of isothermal surfaces for a fixed $(\lambda, \mu)$ and the multiplicative nonzero constants $\mathbb{C}^*$ that scale solutions of the associated ODE. Additionally, we detail transformations of $(\lambda, \mu)$ that yield new isothermal surfaces and explicitly provide the governing differential equations for these cases. Particular attention is given to instances where $(\lambda, \mu)$ are differential forms derived from Darboux or Calapso transformations acting on a standard flat metric on $\Sigma$.

This study introduces a class of semi-parametric estimators for conditional expectation functions within a univariate framework utilizing one covariate. The methodology combines a univariate kernel density estimator with a kernel regression estimator, whose bandwidth is optimized via data-driven selection. The bandwidth selection process relies on minimizing the integrated squared error of intermediate density and regression estimates, thereby eliminating the need for arbitrary manual tuning. Furthermore, the main estimator achieves the optimal minimax rate of convergence, demonstrating smoothness even with a bandwidth selected through this data-driven approach.

This paper establishes new identities for the $\lambda$-version of the $r$-Stirling numbers of the secondary first kind. The demonstration leverages the Faa di Bruno formula alongside an elementary combinatorial argument to confirm these results.

Knowledge Graphs (KGs) serve as a robust infrastructure for storing entity-relational data, facilitating efficient retrieval and prediction tasks. In domains like recommendation systems, the ability to anticipate relations is crucial for suggesting relevant items to users. However, traditional approaches relying on static or temporal knowledge graphs often struggle with sparsity, failing to accurately forecast relations that lack historical evidence. This study introduces a model that integrates fixed structural patterns with temporal embeddings to enhance predictive performance on both observed and unseen relationships. Specifically, we merge the embeddings of an input entity pair with the embedding of a fixed model to generate a representation for that pair. By applying this method, we can identify the most probable unseen relations associated with an entity. Empirical evaluations on two real-world datasets demonstrate that this proposed approach significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art baselines.

The concept of shift equivalence for graphs and associated matrices was initially developed by Higbie to characterize when one symbolic dynamical system can be transformed into another via an covering map. Although Hillas subsequently demonstrated that shift equivalence does not necessarily preserve conjugacy classes under such mappings (i.e., it is possible for algebraic equivalence to exist without corresponding unitary equivalence), recent investigations have sought to establish conditions under which this implication does hold. This discussion outlines a framework of "generalized shift equivalence" designed to extend existing knowledge regarding these sufficient conditions to cases involving infinite directed graphs and $C^*$-algebras featuring countable, row-finite generators.

Heavy ion collision experiments generate intense magnetic fields alongside the creation of the quark-gluon plasma. This study investigates how such fields influence the heavy quark propagator and the subsequent heavy quark-antiquark propagator. Specifically, we examine heavy quark propagators in an external magnetic background using the general propagator method, subsequently deriving the behavior of the pair based on these results. Furthermore, anisotropic differences in imaginary parts related to heavy quark propagators are analyzed to explore open heavy quark-plasma medium interactions.

Knowledge Graphs (KGs) are increasingly integrated into neural language models to enhance performance on tasks like question answering. However, existing methods that KG-augmented language processing often fail to fully utilize the structured knowledge within KGs or effectively combine it with linguistic capabilities. To address this, we introduce an inquiry-answered system that merges a knowledge-graph-driven inference engine with pre-trained language models. This hybrid approach enables the system to derive answers from both structured facts within the KG and unstructured text. We evaluated our method on the ComplexWebQuestions 2.0 dataset, demonstrating superior performance compared to strong baselines. Additionally, we conducted an analysis of error cases to offer insights into how to further improve future models.

Expansions serve as a vital instrument in high-dimensional combinatorics, yet existing definitions are limited to specific forms. This paper introduces a generalized concept of expansion that encompasses previous variations and establishes novel results for both p-biased probability spaces and high-degree graphs. Furthermore, we introduce new "layered spaces" that act as natural candidates for these broadened definitions, delivering significant improvements over previous bounds in hypercube pairs, specific layered space configurations, and understanding the exact p-bias of the complete bipartite graph $K_{n,n}$.

No-shy (zero-shot) text selection has been made possible through advanced transformer models, eliminating the need for extensive training data or fine-tuning. While recent research suggests enhancing these capabilities with carefully engineered natural language prompts, there remains a lack of comprehensive studies evaluating how different prompts perform across diverse zero-shot selection tasks. This work introduces a thorough evaluation of various prompting strategies for six distinct zero-shot text selection tasks. We utilize state-of-the-art transformer models and measure their effectiveness with both simple and complex prompts. Our findings reveal that simple prompts yield solid baseline results, whereas intricate, sophisticated prompts significantly enhance performance. Additionally, we investigate the selection qualities produced by these models to offer deeper insights into their inherent attributes.

We define a family of $p$-adic Lie algebras, $\mathscr{L}_\rho$, associated with every continuous representation $\rho: G_{\mathbb{Q}} \to GL_n(\mathbb{C})$ of the local ground field Galois group, utilizing the lower central series of the absolute Galois group of an auxiliary local field. We establish several attributes of these algebras, including their Whitehead dimensions and structural properties. Subsequently, we demonstrate how specific Regis's Iwasawa invariants of Selmer groups—regarded as arithmetic objects linked to modular forms and abelian varieties—may be expressed through the underlying topological features of $\mathscr{L}_\rho$.

Detecting multiband microwave and terahertz radiation emitted by quantum devices is vital for characterizing their quantum states. However, conventional detection methods struggle with low signal-to-noise ratios when dealing with weak signals. In this study, we present an improved strategy for identifying weak Rydberg multiterahertz microwaves by employing a deep neural network to analyze audio data from a standard detector. This method enhances detection efficiency by approximately 40% compared to traditional approaches. We anticipate that this framework will facilitate more efficient spectroscopic analysis of future quantum systems.

"Disk instability is a primary driver of starburst activity and supermassive black hole growth in galaxies. Although disk stability is typically evaluated using the specific angular momentum of baryonic matter, recent research indicates that including dark matter in the Bekenstein criterion is essential for spiral galaxies. We present high-resolution (0.3 arcsec) integral field spectroscopy of UGC 8839, a nearby spiral galaxy, to assess its disk stability. Our findings reveal an ultra-stable outer disk, with stability decreasing toward the center, reaching a marginal $Q \approx 1$ at the innermost regions. By applying a method that isolates the gravitational pull of the central black hole, we determined that its mass is $M_{\rm BH} = (1.7 \pm 0.4) \times 10^8 \, M_\odot$. Additionally, we calculated the total baryonic mass distribution, finding $M_{\rm b} = (1.0 \pm 0.1) \times 10^{11} \, M_\odot$ and a half-light radius of $R_{\rm b, 50\%} = 2.6 \pm 0.2$ kpc. Consequently, the central concentration of baryonic mass is $M_{\rm b, 50\%} = 0.45 \pm 0.04$

In quasiregular dynamics, the Hausdorff dimension of the Julia set is a pivotal attribute. While R\"{u}hkenm\"{u}lker established a lower bound of 2.5 for the Julia sets of all quasiregular mappings on ${\mathbb R}^3$, the author provides examples demonstrating that this dimension can exceed any given value and has no upper limit.

This study examines the propagation of gravity waves (GWs) within Mars' lower thermosphere, utilizing a dataset of neutral mass density observations from four spacecraft: Mars Global Surveyor (MGS), Mars Odyssey (ODY), Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO), and Mars Atmosphere and Volatile Evolution (MAVEN). The data were analyzed by applying a 2-D Fourier transform across latitude and local time to a dataset of 2-D wavelet coefficients, which were organized into 2-D maps of spectral power. The resulting maps revealed GWs with periods ranging from 1.5 to 3 hours, extending from 60°N to 60°S between 14:00 and 16:00 local time. The spectral power within these specific periods and times is significantly higher than that of other periods and times. The observed structure of power distribution in this 2-D map aligns with the theoretical prediction of GWs spreading equatorward from the two-day tidal wave. Furthermore, the MAVEN results indicate that the amplitude of the 2-day tidal wave and the associated gravity wave activity are greater during the southern hemisphere's summer.

Ultra-peripheral Pb--Pb collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) represent a unique environment for investigating coherent photoproduction of $J/\psi$ mesons, where the interactions are driven by the strong electromagnetic fields of the lead nuclei. This study examines forward $J/\psi$ meson generation in Pb--Pb collisions utilizing data from the ALICE experiment recorded during Run 2 ($\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02$ TeV). Measurements were taken in rapidity intervals of $2.5 < y < 3.5$ and $3.5 < y < 4.6$ within centralities ranging from 0--5% to 80--90%. The transverse momentum distributions were measured up to $p_{\rm T} = 4$ GeV/$c$. These findings are contrasted with predictions from various theoretical frameworks, specifically photon-photon and gluon-gluon fusion models. Furthermore, the data are analyzed in the context of nuclear modifications to both photon flux and gluon distribution.

This study addresses the challenge of generating music through visual guidance, a task that is notoriously difficult due to the highly under-constrained nature of audio production combined with the lack of clear, unambiguous criteria for evaluation. To address these hurdles, the research establishes both a human benchmark and multiple large-scale synthetic datasets, alongside defined metrics for assessing both perceptual and perceptivity quality. With these resources, the authors introduce a baseline model utilizing a GAN framework enhanced with several vision encoders to facilitate training. The released datasets and evaluation metrics are intended to provide a foundation for further investigation into vision-driven audio creation, potentially fostering more innovative and unconventional approaches in the field.

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are renowned for their capacity to model sequential dependencies, a trait that has made them a standard for processing time-series data. However, the training of these networks is often hindered by slow convergence and the vanishing gradient problem. This paper introduces a new training strategy designed to enhance the temporal learning capabilities of RNNs. We name this approach "Temporal Difference Learning" (TDL), a term inspired by the well-established reinforcement learning methodology. By constructing a specialized reward function within TDL, we enable the network to acquire time-aware knowledge, effectively harnessing future information to refine current decisions. Employing this training framework on the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) variant yields the Time Difference LSTM (TD-LSTM). Experimental results indicate that this new approach not only outperforms standard TDL implementations within the network but also delivers superior accuracy compared to conventionally trained LSTM models.

The rapid spread of infectious diseases like SARS-CoV-2 necessitates immediate, well-informed containment measures. While the impact of such actions on epidemic dynamics has been extensively analyzed, their effect on economic outcomes remains less understood. This study utilizes a precise analytical framework to demonstrate that timely implementation of measures significantly delays the peak of an epidemic, thereby diminishing total infections and financial costs. Our findings reveal a remarkable consistency across nations: initiating responses early reduces cumulative infections by 40–50% and curtails economic losses by 40–60%. Furthermore, the results indicate that the speed of implementation is more critical than the strict intensity of the policy. Finally, we observe that the specific choice of measures matters little compared to timing, as long as the approach is enacted promptly.

Ensuring the reliability of machine learning models depends heavily on the trustworthiness of their data pipelines. Although existing methods exist for individual data quality checks, mechanisms for troubleshooting entire data workflows are currently missing. To address this, we introduce **Signatory**, a novel system designed to attribute end-to-end data workflows by identifying and ranking the most significant data issues that impact model performance. Signatory achieves this by integrating workflow execution monitoring with state-of-the-art machine learning techniques. It leverages **SHAP** (Shapley Additive Explanations) to quantify the impact of specific data problems on model predictions and utilizes **Bayesian Gaussian Process (BGP)** regression to efficiently simulate ML model retraining across numerous hypothetical data troubleshooting scenarios. Empirical evaluations using real-world industrial data workflows demonstrate that Signatory delivers more precise workflow attribution than leading baseline approaches, all while requiring a fraction of the computational resources needed for exact methods.

This paper examines the challenges and potential avenues in enumerative geometry, with particular attention to how cutting-edge theoretical physics influences these fields, followed by a specific analysis of tropical geometry and its application to enumerative problems.

This study investigates the pressure-induced transition in Mn$_3$Sn, specifically focusing on how it affects the emergence of a quantized anomalous Hall effect (QAHE) in this kagome Heusler alloy. Under ambient pressure, Mn$_3$Sn exhibits a low-temperature antiferromagnetic phase transition at 150 K, whereas applying 0.5 GPa of pressure shifts this magnetic transition down to 115 K. Furthermore, the zero-field Hall resistivity ($R_{xy}$) shows enhanced negative values at 5 K when pressurized to 0.5 GPa, indicating a strengthened QAHE. Analysis of temperature-dependent $R_{xy}$ suggests that the QAHE originates from the thermal breaking of time-reversal symmetry coupled with the material's non-collinear antiferromagnetic order. Additionally, the study confirms that pressurized samples exhibit a lower critical temperature for the trimerization phase, a state characterized by a 3-fold rotational symmetry in the magnetic structure.

This paper examines recent advances in deep neural network architectures for relation extraction, a core component of knowledge base completion. Following a brief overview of the task, we analyze and compare various models, highlighting their respective advantages and disadvantages. We conclude by addressing current challenges and proposing potential avenues for future research.

The text outlines a Steklov-Robin type problem defined by the Laplace equation $ \Delta u = 0 $ within the unit ball $ B_1 \subset \mathbb{R}^n $ ($ n \geq 3 $), subject to the boundary condition $ \alpha u + \beta \partial_{\nu} u + \gamma |u|^{p-1} u = \sigma $ on $ S^{n-1} $, where $ \alpha, \beta, \gamma $ are real constants, $ \sigma \in C^{\infty}(S^{n-1}) $, and $ p > 1 $. The first positive eigenvalue $ \lambda_1 $ associated with the nonlinear Dirichlet problem $ \Delta u + \lambda |u|^{p-1} u = 0 $ in $ B_1 $ with $ u = 1 $ on $ S^{n-1} $ serves as a critical threshold for the Steklov-Robin problem. The analysis demonstrates that if $ \lambda_c > \lambda_1 $, positive classical solutions exist; conversely, if $ \lambda_c \leq \lambda_1 $, positive solutions are nonexistent.

In the field of image restoration, hypergraphs have proven effective for modeling multi-channel interactions and facilitating restoration across all channels simultaneously. Nevertheless, to the best of our knowledge, no restoration-free guided hypergraph construction method currently exists. Restoring a degraded image to obtain a sharp reference is typically the standard preliminary step for creating such a hypergraph. To address this gap, we introduce a restoration-unnecessary guided hypergraph framework. The core innovation involves a multi-task self-supervised contrastive learning strategy that jointly optimizes the hypergraph structure and the restoration task in an unsupervised, end-to-end manner. Specifically, a shared encoder first extracts features from both clean and degraded image pairs. Subsequently, two separate decoder pathways are utilized: one reconstructs the degraded inputs, while the other builds the hypergraph from the encoded features. Finally, two loss functions are employed to jointly train these components. The first is a multi-task loss that prioritizes both restoration quality and contrastive learning objectives. Complementing this is a contrastive learning objective designed to ensure that feature encodings from paired images maintain discriminative power, thereby preventing information redundancy. Extensive experiments across various scenarios demonstrate that the proposed method not only outperforms state-of-the-art restoration techniques but also constructs high-fidelity guided hypergraphs for image restoration.

Automated systems for analyzing chest radiographs are increasingly vital for public health, especially given the necessity of rapid, large-scale screening during emerging infectious outbreaks. However, existing computer vision models often struggle to match radiologists in accuracy and reliability. Our study introduces Radiology-QA, a novel, high-fidelity dataset featuring 1,000 high-resolution chest X-rays with comprehensive annotations covering disease labels, quantitative measurements, and region-specific information. These multi-dimensional markers were created by synthesizing inputs from multiple expert radiologists to ensure consistency and depth. To validate our annotation strategy, we implemented and tested several state-of-the-art algorithms for quantitative feature extraction. Furthermore, we developed a unique projection technique that reconstructs our 2D radiographic images in 3D space using CT data to verify the anatomical and diagnostic accuracy of our measurements. We have made this dataset publicly available to encourage future research in radiographic analysis.

We define the "Thurston norm" for contact frameworks to extend the established notion applicable to surfaces. Given a closed, oriented surface $\Sigma$ embedded in a contact 3-manifold $(M,\xi)$ with non-zero self-intersection, this norm quantifies the minimum absolute Euler characteristic among all spanning singular disk complexes where $\Sigma$ serves as the boundary. We demonstrate that the resulting norm is piecewise continuous and supply several characterizations of its units. Furthermore, we explore how this norm correlates with existing invariants regarding contact frameworks and provide specific examples and conjectures concerning norm realizable data.

The development of compact light sources emitting stable light in a single direction is a critical requirement for various optical applications. To evaluate the performance of microcavity lasers, we compare the entropy of their radiation patterns. Results indicate that although these systems generally exhibit low beam quality due to complex multi-mode behavior, there exists an entropic threshold below which highly directional beams are achieved.

This study examines the stability of cryptocurrency pricing by integrating two theoretical frameworks: the Law of One Price (LOP) and the Law of Large Numbers (LLN). When evaluated against US Dollar prices, both Bitcoin and Ethereum demonstrated consistent price stability from 2015 to 2022, with similar results observed for Ethereum priced in Chinese Yuan from 2017 to 2022. These empirical findings support the application of the Law of One Price, suggesting that adopting a cryptocurrency as a unit of account is viable. Furthermore, the research investigates how cryptocurrency pricing behaves using an inter-currency approach, confirming that prices across different currencies cluster together, which reinforces the finding that selecting a specific cryptocurrency as a medium of exchange introduces minimal friction.

The broad class of nonlinear partial differential equations known as integrable systems admits a rigorous derivation via inverse scattering methods. A notable example is the derivation of universal scaling exponents for the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) equation from a nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) model, as reported by Sasai and others in *Nature Communications* (2017). Building on this, the authors of the present work apply the inverse scattering technique to the reverse-time NLS (rSP) framework to analyze fluctuations around a steady state in integrable KPZ models. By establishing a one-to-one correspondence between rSP and the Burgers equation, the study reveals that the probability density function (PDF) of height fluctuations in integrable KPZ models is fully determined by the initial PDF. Specifically, at long wavelengths, these heights converge to a Gaussian distribution. This finding aligns with earlier numerical simulations and theoretical arguments suggesting Gaussian behavior based on the ergodic hypothesis. Furthermore, the derived short- and long-time asymptotics of the PDF match existing long-standing conjectures regarding time-scale separability. Ultimately, the rSP scattering approach provides a potent framework for investigating the temporal and spatial dynamics of integrable KPZ systems.

Comprehensive simulations of compressive turbulence in the solar wind reveal that the cascade reaches compressive kinetic scales, triggering plasma shocks and facilitating energy dissipation. Although these simulations predict such activity, actual in-situ observations of compressive motions at these small scales remain scarce. This study examines data from the Magnetospheric Multiscale (MMS) spacecraft to determine if compressive turbulent activity exists near the corresponding kinetic scales in the solar breeze. We analyze three distinct time intervals of solar wind data, utilizing both the Fast Plasma Investigation (FPI) and Acceleration, Composition, and Structure (ACCS) instruments on MMS to identify compressive structures within the 100–1000 Hz frequency band. The identified events are further evaluated against criteria for plasma shocks established by the Vlasov Particle-in-Cell (VPI) simulation referenced in our work. Results indicate that plasma shocks are frequently observed in the solar breeze at scales where turbulent compressibility becomes significant, with roughly 10% of compressive structures at these scales meeting the shock criteria. These findings suggest that the solar breeze exhibits shock activity at sub-ion scales where turbulence is compressive, offering observational backing for the role of shocks in the turbulent energy dissipation process.

The generation of isolated attosecond pulses via High Harmon Generation (HHG) is typically achieved using few-cycle infrared pulses to drive the process. In this study, we introduce a novel method for creating such few-cycle infrared pulses using a modified chirp-taper technique. This alteration involves modulating the amplitude of a tapered beam with a square-wave pattern during propagation through a gas cell. Our numerical simulations demonstrate that a laser beam featuring both positive and negative chirps results in significantly shorter pulse durations compared to using a singly chirped beam. Furthermore, we assessed the impact of finite beam thickness on pulse characteristics and assessed the feasibility of applying this method within X-ray Free-Electron Lasers (FELs) to produce isolated attosecond bursts in the XUV and soft X-ray spectral ranges.

We introduce a tangential optical method to determine the viscosity of stratified viscous fluids undergoing shear flow. This approach involves projecting a laser sheet tangentially into the flow, capturing the resulting illuminated plane with a co-located camera, and measuring the magnification change around tracer particles. The experimental arrangement was validated against Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) within a viscous flume experiment simulating a shear-driven stratified boundary layer. Results demonstrated that this technique successfully estimates both velocity profiles and viscosity, achieving an accuracy of approximately 20% compared to PIV measurements.

Gerrymandering represents a manipulation of electoral district boundaries that skews election results without altering voter preferences. Although numerous methods exist for detecting such manipulation, they typically fail to address cases involving multi-party systems. This work introduces an algorithm capable of generating samples of redistricting maps for any number of parties, with utility ranging from producing samples to assessing the probability of specific maps and quantifying gerrymandering severity. The proposed approach relies on a Markov chain Monte Carlo technique driven by simulated annealing, where elevated temperatures facilitate transitions between map configurations that would otherwise be inaccessible. The resulting framework allows researchers to evaluate the likelihood of any given map and derive confidence intervals for gerrymandering metrics. Applied to Texas maps spanning from 1992 to 2002, the method reveals that while historical maps exhibited less severe gerrymandering than legally mandated maps for the subsequent two decades, the difference lacks statistical significance.

Flaw identification in textile images is crucial for quality control within the industry. While human inspectors remain prevalent, their tendency toward fatigue-induced errors highlights the urgent need for automated alternatives. However, existing automated systems often struggle with the specific characteristics of textile images, particularly the high similarity between flaws and normal patterns, leading to subpar performance in current methodologies. To address this, we introduce a new Gabor-Haar cascaded Gabor pyramid (GHOG) descriptor that effectively captures local image features. Furthermore, leveraging the inherent low-rank structure of patterned images, we integrate this GHOG descriptor with a matrix completion approach for flaw detection. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms both traditional techniques and state-of-the-art solutions in real-world applications.

This research introduces a new visual navigation framework grounded in information theory. It combines data-driven regularizations, such as mutual information and the information bottleneck principle, to enhance learned representations and regulate policy complexity. By optimizing these mutural information-based objectives, a policy is derived that achieves significant improvements in both navigation success rates and sample efficiency. Additionally, the proposed method supports unsuper-vised pre-training, a stage that markedly boosts subsequent supervised performance. Empirical evaluations across various benchmarks, including the R2R challenge, the Microsoft Virtual Router (Virtual-Router), and AI2-Home, confirm the effectiveness of these approaches.

We investigate binary systems within galactic nuclei, specifically focusing on globular clusters and dwarf galaxies, to determine their gravitational wave emission. Our findings indicate that in systems hosting a black hole of $10^6$ to $10^7$ M$_{\odot}$, the resulting gravitational wave signals are detectable by LISA and the Einstein Telescope. These signals originate from diverse sources, including supermassive black hole binaries, high-mass X-ray binaries, low-mass X-ray binaries, and binaries involving stellar-mass black holes. Notably, we identify a prominent peak in the source distribution at frequencies of 0.1 to 1 Hz, corresponding to the final inspiral and merger phases of high-mass X-ray binaries. This finding suggests that the merger rate of these binaries could rival that of standard field binaries. Consequently, analyzing these specific high-frequency peaks in LISA data could provide valuable insights into the formation and evolutionary history of binary systems inside galactic nuclei.

Power system operators are increasingly prioritizing the identification of in-grid events, such as faults and switching operations, to enhance system safety and equipment integrity. However, existing methods relying on extensive datasets of historical signals often fail to function effectively in data-scarce environments. This study introduces a novel approach for detecting power measurement events that utilizes a data-driven framework built on variational mode decomposition (VMD) and the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence measure. First, KL divergence is calculated between the mode specific components derived from VMD to highlight significant transient variations. Building on this insight, a data-informed mechanism is implemented to identify historical baseline information, thereby reducing the data volume required for effective operation. Furthermore, a counterexample involving synthetic signals demonstrates the approach's efficacy, with additional validation achieved through analysis of real-world electrical arc measurements.

This paper investigates the proposed $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ transition, which serves as a critical component of the aforementioned $J/\psi \pi \pi \delta$ decay mechanism. We employ the hadronic molecular model to forecast the branching ratio for $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ and its associated form. We present a categorical characterization of the Hom-worksheet for the Veronese embedding, $v_d:\mathbb{P}^{n} \to \mathbb{P}^{N}$, where $d\geq 2$ and $\mathbb{P}^n$ is governed by projective space. This study extends prior research by Buan and S\"{u}l{\uacute}k (2009), who provided a similar description for the quadratic Veronese map. Our findings further explore the global properties of these embedded projective spaces and their associated homogeneous ideals.

Text-based games offer an open domain for research, yet their search efficiency remains constrained by slow interpretation, typically allowing only tens of actions per second. This paper introduces TextWorldExpress, an efficient C++ implementation optimized for search that achieves a performance leap of four orders of magnitude—reaching over one million moves per second—by replacing slow Python virtual interpreter execution with a fast C++ simulated engine. This advancement enables deeper and more effective exploration of the game state space.

We introduce a novel geometric methodology designed to determine the spin texture of Topological Insulators (TIs) that exhibit defects. In this approach, conduction electrons are mapped onto the spin-1/2 representation of the $SU(2)$ group, where the mapping's orientation is dictated by the specific spin texture. By calculating how Bloch states transform under an infinitesimal $SU(2)$ rotation, we identify the corresponding $SU(2)$ spin-1/2 axes for any flawed TI. The demonstration of this method occurs within the defect scenario for a $Bi_2Se_3$ slab, where we observe that spin textures gradually evolve from radial to tangential as they transition from the surface toward the defect center.

We examine $p$-harmonic functions within two-dimensional non-diverging sectors, establishing upper and lower bounds on their absolute values along with their first and second derivatives. Our analysis demonstrates that the absolute convergence of these functions depends on their behavior at specific boundary points, provided $1<p<\infty$. Furthermore, we prove that first derivative convergence always holds when $1<p<q<\infty$, while the convergence of the second derivatives is guaranteed for the range $2<p$.

This paper introduces a new multivariate spatial model designed to simulate extreme multi-dimensional environments conditioned on specific thresholds. The proposed framework extends the univariate approach by Bérard et al. (2018), which relies on generalized Pareto distributions (GPDs) and their spatial dependencies, to spatially correlated d-dimensional datasets. The modeling strategy decomposes the space into two components: the marginal peaks of interest and the conditional structure, representing the state given they exceed certain limits. The parameters for the conditional structure are linked through variograms derived from Bérard and Cooley (2016) and co-authors. The model's validity is demonstrated using simulated data and a case study analyzing extreme wave heights and significant wave directions.

We examine bounded, non-constant rational maps $X \to \mathbb{G}_m$ defined and regular over the ring of integers in a number field, where $X$ varies within a fixed family of varieties. Our findings demonstrate that such maps take only finitely many values whenever they are sufficiently small, provided the variety's dimension is at least 2. Furthermore, we extend these results to non-constant maps targeting semisimple algebraic groups for varieties with dimension no greater than 2.

This study introduces a new collaborative paradigm where a human and a robot work together to adjust a manipulator's pose. Driven by a shared goal of reaching a specific target object, the human guides the end-effuator along a manifold while the robot executes an ICP algorithm constrained to that same manifold. Unlike traditional setups, the human provides an extra degree of freedom, allowing the manipulator to achieve the target using fewer degrees of its own. To account for variations caused by human movement, we define a new metric: "manifold-aware injectability." Furthermore, we develop a manifold-aware ICP method that performs manifold projection during both the minimization and maximization steps. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach enables smoother adjustments and more efficient reaching of target objects across various scenarios.

This study examines the Standard Model Higgs boson pair production via the $\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ and $\textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}$ decay channels at the LHC, utilizing the matrix element technique to analyze event topology. Distinguishing features of the top-loop induced $\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ sub-process from the Fermi $\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ sub-process are investigated. Event topologies are further categorized by the invariant mass of the $\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ system, enhancing the sensitivity to contributions arising from a Higgs self-coupling mediated by top quarks.

We introduce Unintentional Turntables, a method for learning 3D object detection and pose estimation without requiring paired training images. This system utilizes large-scale image collections that contain natural camera movements resembling a table rotating an object in all directions. By analyzing these collections, we can train a 3D position and orientation estimator for an object class by detecting a single example of that class per image. To achieve this, the system employs a 3D position estimator trained on a generated "turntable dataset," where a single prototype object is rendered in various rotations against a uniform background. This estimator is then adapted to real-world scenes by identifying an image translation that maximizes the estimated 3D position of an estimated object. Experiments demonstrate that this approach effectively estimates 3D positions in data featuring single examples per image and outperforms current state-of-the-art methods for multi-view stereo on standard benchmarks.

The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has intensified the spread of misinformation, particularly regarding the vaccines. This study introduces a novel task: distinguishing whether individuals accept or reject misinformation in Twitter conversations. We assembled the first publicly available dataset comprising 1,000 tweet excerpts, each featuring a pair of consecutive user replies to misinformation posts related to the vaccines. These annotations provide four critical elements: the source of the misinformation, the misinformation claim itself, the user's acceptance status, and the user's refusal status. We propose a method that leverages the sequential dialogue context to identify these acceptance and refusal states. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms strong baselines, including models that ignore sequential context.

Generating isolated attosecond pulses (IAPs) is pivotal for probing ultrafast electron dynamics in matter, a capability that has been hindered by challenges in both theoretical and experimental IAP generation. This study demonstrates that robustly tailored mid-infrared fields can effectively control IAP creation in xenon atoms, yielding a 30-attosecond duration pulse with strong amplitude and phase stability. The proposed method offers a practical pathway for producing IAPs, thereby advancing efforts to investigate electron motion in complex environments.

The ground-based APOGEE survey has identified a candidate Algol-type eclipsing binary system, designated APOGEE J1626-0048, which is located within the Cygnus OB2 association. This system comprises a primary star of spectral type G2IV with a mass of 2.62 ± 0.15 M$_{\odot}$, and a secondary of mass 0.36 ± 0.06 M$_{\odot}$. The companion's spectral features are too faint to classify, though its low mass suggests it is likely a brown dwarf or very low-mass star. The system's orbital period is 2.6 days, and the inclination is nearly edge-on at 89.5°. While the discovery was made via APOGEE data, the system was not included in the final DR14 release due to the presence of a significant secondary eclipse dip that could skew the radial velocity measurements. This study presents follow-up observations from the Lick 2.3m telescope, which reveal a secondary eclipse feature in the optical light curve and indicate that the companion's emission is detectable in near-infrared bands. The derived bolometric luminosity for the companion is approximately 10$^{-4}$ L$_{\odot}$. We examine the nonlinear Schrödinger equation within the exterior of a convex obstacle in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$, where Dirichlet conditions are applied on the obstacle's surface. Under specific assumptions, we establish that explosion-type solutions exist for this problem.

Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have proven effective for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) across various fields. However, training PINN on high-dimensional PDEs remains computationally expensive and often yields inaccurate results due to their inability to satisfy the PDE throughout the entire domain. This study introduces Residual-driven Adaptive Node Generation (RANG), a novel method for dynamically adding training nodes in regions with high PDE error. The approach estimates local PDE error to prioritize sampling in under-resolved areas, thereby enhancing solution accuracy. Furthermore, a multi-strategy sampling technique is employed to prevent early sampling from biasing later data selection. Numerical experiments on both linear and non-linear PDEs demonstrate that RANG significantly outperforms existing adaptive sampling techniques by achieving high precision with far fewer training nodes.

This study presents the implementation and analysis of a novel multi-domain physics model integrated with a drift-diffusion simulator, specifically designed to investigate ferroelectric devices exhibiting domain wall Negative Capacitance (NC) phenomena. By dynamically simulating multiple domain walls within the NC region, we accurately capture shifts in NC behavior. We initially validate the simulator using a vertical 2D superlattice model, demonstrating its ability to locate domain walls and plot the NC region. Subsequently, we analyze an n-type Ferroelectric Field-Effect Transistor (FET) structured with an S-shaped path, revealing domain wall NC effects and verifying the device's capability to leverage wall-driven NC for performance enhancement. Ultimately, we examine the 3D morphology of domain walls and NC in the transistor, revealing that domain orientation significantly influences both the NC behavior and the overall device performance.

This study introduces a novel, multi-layer, multi-attribute graph framework designed to represent freight ecosystems, enabling the evaluation of network fragility through experiments on the United States. The proposed multi-layer graph integrates data on freight carriers, network infrastructure, and regulatory policies, while its multi-attribute design captures the specific nature of relationships between entities and the attributes of those relationships. To facilitate a comprehensive understanding of the network, the authors developed FreightFG, a dedicated freight development platform that combines the insight graphs with a visual interface. Utilizing FreightFG, the study executed a fragility spread experiment, analyzing how disruptions propagate across freight carriers, network infrastructure, and policy environments within the broader ecosystem.

In this study, the ergodicity of the stochastic intricate Ginzburg-Landau (iGL) equation, a system influenced by noise containing pure jump disturbances, is established by proving its irreducibility and establishing an irreducibility result. To this end, the martingale problem associated with the equation's operator is first analyzed, yielding strong solutions in the $L^2$ space under periodic boundary conditions. Furthermore, irreducibility is demonstrated through a specific approximation method. Subsequently, an ergodic property is proved for the stochastic iGL equation driven by subordinator noise with sublinear diffusion and additive pure jump noise. Finally, the ergodicity of the corresponding Markov semigroup is derived, effectively determining the long-term behavior of the equation.

This paper determines the minimal degree of simple power graphs $\mathcal{G}^{\times}_G$ when $G$ is a nilpotent group, noting previous authors failed to provide a straightforward criterion for this value in such cases. Our findings establish this least minor degree for all power graphs associated with abelian-by-square nilpotent groups, effectively characterizing them as characterizing by their least degree of power graphs in these specific nilpotent contexts.

This paper introduces a new hadron spectrometer designed to address two primary objectives: first, conducting precision measurements of hadronic cross-sections and scattering amplitudes in the low transverse momentum ($p_T < 1$ GeV/$c$) regime to enhance inputs for hadronic cross-section models used in heavy-ion collision simulations; second, performing extensive measurements of particle correlations and event structures to generate comprehensive datasets that will significantly improve understanding of event developments in cosmic rays.

Point cloud data, which captures the three-dimensional geometry of objects, is widely used in fields like robotics and augmented reality. While Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have emerged as a leading architecture for processing point clouds by constructing graphs based on inter-point relationships, they often struggle with over-smoothing when applied to large-scale 3D data. This issue stems from the standard use of Euclidean distance, which fails to account for global geometric context. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that builds graph connectivity using an adaptive, learnable distance metric. Empirical results demonstrate that this method significantly mitigates over-smoothing, yielding superior performance in point cloud classification and segmentation.

Recent advancements in deep learning have introduced novel Deep Learning Stratosphere Hostless Trojans (DLSHTs), which outperform earlier models by reducing detection difficulty while enhancing evasion capabilities. The current study introduces a new class, the Semantic DLSHT, targeting segmentation networks. The proposed methodology modifies model predictions by integrating trojan subgraphs into the semantics of segmentation networks via trojan words, thereby inducing specific assault effects. The implementation requires only a minimal number of trigger pixels and necessates no labeled training data. The presented framework is general and easily extensible to other deep learning applications. The methodology was validated on leading semantic segmentation models, specifically DeDe and DeepLabv2, using the Cityscapes dataset. The results demonstrate an improvement of 20% over the most advanced DLSHT, achieving high accuracy rates for both trigger size and assault precision.

The Re-Observatory System for Integral-field Imaging (ROSIE) represents a new integral-field instrument (IFU) designed to operate within the Las Cumbres Observatory Global Telescope (LCCT) network. This system aims to capture high-resolution, wide-field data across the optical spectrum, enabling the simultaneous observation of both spatial and spectral data across diverse celestial sources. To achieve this, ROSIE employs a custom IFU built from a micro-electro-mechanical system (MEMS) micromirror array coupled with a high-throughput, multi-object spectrograph. This approach leverages existing multi-object instrumentation to target a wide field of view while utilizing mature MEMS mirror technology to achieve fine spatial sampling. Developed under the guidance of the National Science Foundation's (NSF) Major Equipment Grants (MEG) program, the instrument is being engineered to serve as a versatile platform for a wide array of scientific investigations. This article details the design, construction, and initial testing phases of the device, outlining its current status and future developmental plans.

This study reviews the current status of carbon-carbon nuclear fusion at extremely low energies and introduces a newly developed variation of the Trojan Horse Sketch (THT) technique. Using this modified THT approach, researchers successfully separated the entrance channel dynamics from reaction dynamics within existing experimental data. By applying three-body quantum dynamics theory to this configuration, the absolute fusion cross-sections were reconstructed across a spectrum of energies. These reconstructed fusion cross-sections were then compared against conventional model predictions to evaluate various theoretical frameworks. The primary innovation of this methodology lies in its capacity to precisely determine long-range components of the nucleon-nucleon force by disentangling entrance from reaction mechanisms, a feat unachievable through present theoretical models alone when dealing with extremely low-energy fusion interactions.

We present high-resolution, high-signal-to-noise ratio spectroscopic data for 12 planet-host stars, utilizing the ESPRESSo instrument at the Very Large Telescope. Our analysis measured the abundances of 13 elements in these stars and compared them with recent estimates of volatile core compositions for super-Earthers and Earth-like planets derived from studies by Weiss et al. (2018) and Weiss & Weiss (2018). The resulting correlations between stellar photospheric abundances and predicted core values are strong, with coefficients of determination ($r^2$) ranging from 0.80 to 0.99. This strong agreement supports the hypothesis that convective zone material reflects core accreting matter, implying that the chemical makeup of terrestrial-type exoplanet cores mirrors that of their forming solar nebula.

Commercial Wireless Positioning (WP) systems utilize Channel State Information (CSI) to determine locations within indoor environments. Nevertheless, multipath effects introduce distortions into CSI that compromise positioning accuracy. Addressing this, we propose a novel attention-based multipath filter designed to recover distorted CSI signals. The core mechanism leverages the observation that CSI amplitudes follow a Laplacian distribution, employing an attention mechanism to dynamically weight CSI sub-carriers based on this distribution profile. The resulting filtered signal is then employed for high-precision positioning. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques in both multipath mitigation and accuracy, achieving a root mean square error (RMSE) as low as 0.44 meters.
