As a concrete application, we derive a set of BPS saturation conditions for transverse excitations of these transitorily moving D1-D5 branes.

In 2017, the authors introduced the problem of determining the minimum polynomials required to compute the duration of a specific class of symmetric networks, a task they initially hypothesized would necessitate a polynomial of degree $O(N)$. This current paper disproves that conjecture by presenting a counterexample consisting of a network where the minimal polynomial for duration is $O(N^{1/3})$. Furthermore, the study establishes the capability of utilizing Cai-Forer-Immerman graphs to construct such counterexamples, while also presenting an open inquiry concerning the lower bounds for unrestricted polynomial duration in unrestricted, general networks.

The substitution of bismuth for europium in pyrochlore iridates, Eu$_{1-x}$Bi$_{x}$Ir$_{2}$O$_{7}$, is analyzed here using hard X-ray photoemission spectroscopy. As the Bi concentration increases, a shift in Eu$^{3+}$ 4f core-level spectra toward Bi$^{3+}$ core levels is observed, confirming the formation of Bi$^{3+}$ species. Simultaneously, the valence band spectra evolve from a configuration characterized by Eu 5d and Ir 5d orbitals to one dominated by Bi 6p and Ir 5d orbitals. Notably, the emergence of Bi 6p states is accompanied by a significant reduction in electron density within the crucial energy range of 0–2 eV. This reduction correlates with a transition from an insulating to a conducting state, suggesting that Bi doping facilitates a switch from an insulating 5d-based electronic structure to a hybridized 6p–5d regime.

This paper introduces a new concept of the "heart" for n-dimensional subsets within a Euclidean space, defined as the collection of all "good" points where the boundary exhibits an infinite number of arbitrarily small oscillations. We demonstrate that for any Lipschitz single-valued function $f$ from a compact subset of $\mathbb{R}^m$ to $\mathbb{R}^n$ (where $m \geq 2$), the set of its non-continuous points has a "heart" that constitutes the entire preimage of the oscillation set $O_f$. Additionally, we establish that for any compact set-valued function $F$ from a compact domain in $\mathbb{R}^m$ to $\mathbb{R}^n$ (again with $m \geq 2$), the "heart" of the set $O_F$ fully captures the preimage of $O_F$ under the projection to the selection of $F$'s discontinuity points. Leveraging these findings along with additional technical results, we develop multiple new methods for determining the Hölder continuity of continuous selections for compact set-valued functions $F$ on compact domains in $\mathbb{R}^m$. These approaches include both algorithmic procedures capable of verifying this property and equivalent conditions that characterize when Lipschitz choices for $F$ exist.

We demonstrate that for every positive integer $n \geq 3$, there exists a nontransitive likelihood relation defined on a set of $n$ alternatives. Additionally, we show there is no circular preference relation involving $n$ alternatives for which the likelihood of strict preference between any two distinct alternatives is uniform across all pairs. As a corollary, it follows that equal likelihoods of strict preference among $n$ alternatives ($n \geq 3$), as proposed by Bradley (2007), do not preclude the possibility of such relations being inconsistent.

In object-oriented programming, virtual function calls typically incur performance overhead compared to static binding due to the need to locate the function address at runtime. To mitigate this, researchers have explored techniques that replace dynamic dispatch with compile-time resolution, often referred to as virtual dispatch elimination. However, many existing solutions fail to account for the Run-Time Setup (RTSU) phase—a mechanism where objects are initialized with setup code before entering the main program flow. Since functions invoked during RTSU must remain accessible dynamically, these solutions currently offer no performance advantage over standard virtual dispatch in this specific context. This paper presents the first systematic investigation comparing the efficacy of eliminating virtual dispatch specifically within the RTSU stage. We analyze how this elimination impacts both the runtime performance of the main program flow and the total program execution time, considering the functions' usage patterns. Furthermore, we evaluate the sensitivity of dispatch removal strategies to code distribution and propose the Compile-Time Setup (CTS) system, designed to streamline function removal across dispatch sites within RTSU. Experimental results demonstrate that applying CTS yields an average speedup of 1.22x for the RTSU phase, resulting in an overall program execution time reduction of 6.4%.

Direct detection experiments for light dark matter (DM) typically focus on nuclear recoil, where the signal is overwhelmed by background noise. This study demonstrates that even for light DM candidates, electron recoils within the lattice of a nucleus can serve as a primary detection channel. By examining the sub-GeV regime, we reveal that when the dark matter particle's mass falls below roughly 100 MeV, the resulting electronic recoil becomes the leading signature, surpassing nuclear recoil in rate. Consequently, experiments utilizing this phase-space can significantly extend their reach into higher dark matter masses. We further analyze the specific advantages of using liquid xenon and propose innovative analysis techniques to substantially lower signal thresholds. Ultimately, observing dark matter via these low-energy electron recoils offers a robust strategy for directly detecting light dark matter particles amidst significant cosmological abundance.

We examine two variations of the anti-Jaynes-Cummings model, investigating energy exchange oscillations, entanglement dynamics, and photon transmission coefficients. It is observed that both configurations exhibit oscillatory energy exchange, and their capacity to generate entanglement reaches a constant maximum during these fluctuations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the photon transmission coefficient equals unity whenever oscillatory peaks for energy or entanglement occur.

This study introduces a new algorithm designed to calculate Inter-Beat Intervals (IBIs) with heightened precision. The proposed method utilizes a specific combination of the Tiramisu framework alongside the autocorrelation algorithm. Validation was performed using the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, which yielded an overall Root Mean Square Deviation (RMSSD) of 13.33 ms. The system was further tested on the Physionet dataset, achieving an RMSSD of 13.33 ms. The findings indicate that the algorithm is particularly effective in environments characterized by noisy signals.

Active matter systems are defined by their self-propulsion, a characteristic driven by a combination of self-generated forces and internal memory. Within this framework, Labor (the work performed by active agents) serves as a key metric for quantifying self-propulsion. This study examines two mathematical formulations of active self-propulsion: one utilizing an active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle (AUP) framework and the other based on an effective stochastic first-order equation. By analyzing labor in both models, we identify a fundamental discrepancy in their predictions. Specifically, we demonstrate that an apparent contradiction in labor values arises from a non-physical singularity present in the stochastic integral defining the AUP framework. Furthermore, we propose a refined mathematical formulation that resolves this issue and aligns labor calculations across both the AUP and first-order stochastic equations.

Capturing human gestures is vital for applications ranging from sign language recognition and virtual avatars to human-robot interaction and scene understanding. While recent technologies like wearable sensors and depth cameras have enhanced gesture capture capabilities, there remains a lack of extensive public datasets featuring diverse multiview gesture angles and a corresponding benchmark for evaluation. To address this gap, we introduce HUMBI, a novel dataset featuring 130 elderly participants performing 15 distinct English hand gestures, resulting in 1,950 sequences recorded across 11 camera viewpoints at 60 fps using depth cameras. To further challenge current methods, we established a benchmark featuring three difficult tasks—low-light imaging, occluded regions, and uncalibrated multiview reconstruction—accompanied by a contest that spurred novel algorithmic advancements. Finally, we released the open-source HumbiPy toolkit to facilitate this benchmark and ensure fair comparisons, thereby encouraging broader research into human gesture analysis.

Current cross-lingual transfer methods rely heavily on a specific classifier architecture, which limits their architectural flexibility. This study introduces a neural classifier that utilizes weak task depictions, enabling easy cross-lingual transfer with minimal high-quality annotated data requirements. We demonstrate that transferring classifiers, trained on archaic or small datasets, to modern languages is both simple and effective. We introduce a classifier that integrates task embeddings with word embeddings to function as weak guidance, facilitating the transfer of model-independent neural classifiers. This approach treats task embeddings as regulative signals, allowing the classifier to be trained on small datasets and easily transferred to new languages using only a modest amount of high-quality labeled data. Using Sentence Pair Classification as a primary case study, we show that our classifier matches the performance of fine-tuned counterparts on large corpora and performs robustly with datasets as small as 1,000 examples.

The Basical RNN-based BasicVSR model marked a significant milestone in unsupervised video super-resolution (USR) by prioritizing low-level alignment over immediate high-level details. Nevertheless, the inherent sequential nature of Basical RNN-based Video Super-Resolution (USR) often results in the rapid propagation of errors and suboptimal restoration of high-frequency details. To address these limitations, we introduce BasicVSR++, a novel architecture designed to further refine the Balical RNN-based Video Super-Resolution (USR) process. Building upon the Balical RNN-based Video Super-Resolution (USR) framework, we implement two primary enhancements: (1) a new enhanced transmission and alignment (TRA) module that boosts short-term consistency by leveraging self-explained features to guide feature fusion and sharpening; and (2) an updated long-term consistency mechanism that utilizes cross-frame self-explained features to stabilize predictions across an extended temporal window. Extensive experiments confirm that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches on multiple benchmarks, delivering superior super-Resolution results (SR) with higher Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) and Perceptual Quality Index (PQSS). Subjective evaluations also demonstrate that BasicVSR++ offers clearer textures and more natural motion rendering compared to existing techniques.

Research into generalization and transfer within multi-task reinforcement learning (RL) has yielded promising outcomes, demonstrating that effectively learned policies often emerge even without explicit transfer strategies. However, these methods exhibit significant instability, frequently resulting in catastrophic performance fluctuations across different tasks. This paper introduces a novel approach to modular RL system design that mitigates such instability during the multi-task training process while preserving or enhancing sample efficiency. Our methodology employs two key systems: an evaluator module that organizes training by prioritizing currently active learning tasks, and a selectororor module that determines the appropriate policy to execute based on the task's contextual cues. Empirical evidence from both simulated environments and real-world robotic manipulation confirms that our system either matches or surpasses the sample efficiency of standard multi-task training techniques while eliminating performance collapse.

We introduce a finite-duration thermodynamic engine framework that simulates a system's evolution as the concatenation of two distinct phases: one governed by uncontrolled stochastic dynamics, followed by a finite-length control period during which external actions are applied to optimize specific performance metrics. Several illustrative scenarios elucidate the theoretical model, after which the general case is addressed using the Muckenhoupt $\mathcal{M}_p$ theory to demonstrate that optimal strategies exist within the space of admissible control functions of order $p$. Finally, for applications of limited duration where scaling analysis is relevant, our findings reveal that optimal control scales linearly with duration specifically in the large-time asymptotic regime.

Severe storms represent a major driver of spatial-temporal fluctuations in electricity demand, yet current literature has paid little attention to a comprehensive analysis of their specific effects. This study examines the impact of extreme weather events on electricity systems by employing temporal difference-in-difference (DID) methodologies. We utilize data from the National Weather Service (NWS) and the Energy Information Administration (EIA) to isolate storm impacts, finding that the introduction of NWS warnings reduces electricity consumption by an average of 0.4% to 1.2%. Furthermore, we integrate a spatial DID approach to assess the heterogeneous impact of storms across neighboring counties. The results indicate that storm-induced demand reductions are more pronounced in coastal areas and regions with weaker building codes. Spatially, the effect exhibits significant negative first-order autocorrelation but negligible second-order autocorrelation, suggesting that the impact on a specific county is highly dependent on whether an adjacent county experienced a similar reduction.

This work establishes an "three spheres" theorem for eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator within Clifford-valued functions. For these functions, the mean square value over a sphere is governed by a specific combination of values evaluated at three strategically selected nested spheres situated inside it. This finding serves as a powerful tool in proving uniqueness results and three related theorems regarding zero distributions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the existence of a broad class of finite zero polynomials for Clifford-valued Dirac operators' eigenfunctions.

Chaos theory and complex systems are characterized by their sensitivity to initial conditions, a property often quantified using finite-time Lyapunov exponents (FTLEs). Building on the work of Pikovsky and colleagues, we introduce a new methodology for analyzing FTLEs within dynamical systems by applying the Dirac measure to chaos and employing Dany framework concepts. This approach enables the identification of a specific subset of completely developed chaotic states, referred to as "maximally chaotic." We demonstrate that these states correspond to the Dyck measure on binary trees. Furthermore, we investigate how these systems address entropy constraints, specifically examining the conditions under which the "entropy collapse" phenomenon occurs. Our findings reveal that while maxillary chaotic states can theoretically achieve zero approachability of entropy, this property is not a universal trait of all chaotic states. Instead, zero approachability arises only when specific structural requirements are met, providing evidence that the Dyck measure represents just one member of a broader class of measures that satisfy these criteria.

The prospect of discovering a Higgs-like state at the Large Hadron Collider (LHHC) has motivated a rigorous examination of scalar sectors featuring extended Higgs mechanisms. We analyze projected sensitivity for a three-scalar model at LHC Run 2 and future high-energy colliders, specifically the High-Luminosity LHC (luminosity 3 ab$^{-1}$) and a 100 Tep proton collider. Building on previous work, we refine our methodology by incorporating the full covariance matrix of fitted parameters to accurately determine confidence regions in parameter space. We further investigate the feasibility of resolving individual scalar masses within this model. Our results indicate that the High-Luminosity LHC could probe center-of-mass energies up to 14 Tev, while a 100 Tev proton collider would extend this reach to approximately 32 Tev.

This study introduces Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet), a novel pitch-conditioned audio synthesis framework that models raw waveforms autoregressively. To address the extreme difficulty of predicting individual sample probabilities directly, QPNet employs a two-stage strategy. Initially, it utilizes a U-Net architecture to estimate the time-varying pitch contour and log amplitude envelope from conditioning inputs, leveraging the robustness of deep learning for this intermediate step. Subsequently, the waveform generation relies on a Quadratic Dilated Convolution Network (QDCNN) to approximate the probability distribution of waveforms, using the estimated pitch and amplitude as quasi-regressions. This quadratic formulation offers a more efficient and accurate representation of these time-varying characteristics than traditional methods. Experiments demonstrate that QPNet not only generates high-quality sound but also maintains a significantly faster inference speed compared to the baseline WaveNet architecture.

Collaborative filtering (CF) remains a primary technique for addressing the information overload challenge inherent in recommending similar items to users based on similar preferences. However, the inherent subjectiveness, sparsity, and local nature of user preferences often limit CF's effectiveness. This paper introduces a novel Bicluster-based CF (BCCF) framework designed to enhance recommendation quality by leveraging bicluster structures to capture more accurate user-item similarities. A key component of the proposed approach is the integration of local and global biclusters, which refines similarity measurement by distinguishing between users and items within these nested clusters. Furthermore, to boost computational efficiency, we present an optimized version called OBCCCF, which utilizes sparse matrix operations and sparse factorization methods. Empirical evaluations on two real-world datasets demonstrate that the BCECF framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art CF methods, while the BCBCFF and global bicluster configurations surpass bicluster setups relying solely on local clusters.

This study utilizes high-resolution, disk-integrated spectral data from the GONG network and the TESS/2MASS/HARPS-N archives to investigate solar magnetic fields and activity. We demonstrate that the Varying Activity Index (VAI) can be effectively computed from GONG Doppler velocity measurements. Additionally, we introduce the Spectral Variance Index (SVI), a novel marker derived from HARPS-N spectra, which quantifies pixel-by-pixel pixel variance in velocity measurements. Both the VAI and SVI exhibit a strong correlation with the Standard Activity Marker (SAM), represented by GONG spectral variances, as well as with the GONG Doppler Velocity VAI. Furthermore, the SVI shows a clear dependence on solar rotation phases, specifically the longitudinal distribution of magnetic plages and spots. We also examine the relationship between these activity markers and solar irradiance data sourced from TESS.

To effectively distinguish Majorana zero-energy peaks from other interference features in non-ideal tunneling spectroscopy, a new strategy is introduced. This technique employs a resistive (Ohmic) tunning barrier and utilizes inactive superconducting electrodes, offering a more practical alternative to current demanding experimental methods. The underlying mechanism is analyzed through a model incorporating the dynamic resistance of the barrier and the finite impedance of the measurement circuit, demonstrating that a robust signature of Majorana modes emerges even when static energy peaks are smeared out by thermal fluctuations. The proposed experimental setup mirrors existing tunneling spectroscopy arrangements, making it highly feasible to implement. Furthermore, its accessibility and ease of execution make this method a valuable, supplementary tool for the ongoing search for Majorana modes.

This research extends the concept of bicategorical quantifiers to pose "shadow" questions regarding the spatial distribution of shadows within images. We introduce the logical predicate, or "shadow," to bicategories functioning as 2-quanta, enabling the formulation of shadows' shadows within a specific region. As an application, the paper demonstrates how this extended logical framework can be utilized to refine the definition provided by Pieter Abbeel et al. Furthermore, we illustrate the utility of this approach in fine-tuning object detection models, specifically those trained on the COCO dataset.

Although tone mapping has long been a focal point of color science, existing methods typically rely on predefined parameters or automatically applied look-up tables, often neglecting the distinct stylistic nuances found in different images. This study introduces a novel approach to style transfer that combines forward and reverse applications. By employing a four-layer Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to concurrently learn a tone mapping operator and its inverse, the model can effectively separate stylistic cues from the scene content of input images. During training, a dataset is constructed of paired images: one set functions as preprocessed input (style) and the other as dynamically generated output (transmitted tone) derived by applying the forward operator. This architecture ensures a bidirectional relationship where both component models are optimized jointly. For any given input, the system can either synthesize a new style by acting as the tone mapping operator or restore original tones by functioning as its inverse. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that this framework not only achieves state-of-the-art results in standard metric evaluations but also produces high-quality, natural-looking images during both direction-specific inferences.

It begins by detailing the contest background and objectives, then describes the submitted datasets, evaluation protocols, and final results. This study presents the inaugural proof of selective sweeping in atmospheric turbulence, a phenomenon where particles or structures within a flowing medium are swept across a detection plane by velocity selective inertial forces. Conducted using a laser scanning technique, researchers measured the anisotropic temporal scattering of light from snowflakes during various snowfalls, revealing that time series data exhibit scale-dependent characteristics determined by the relative magnitude of two time scales: one representing the duration required to traverse the laser sheet and the other representing the duration for atmospheric advection to move a snowflake across similar scales. When the laser crossing time vastly exceeds the advection time at large scales, light scattering ceases. By adjusting the scale of the virtual probe to match that of the laser intersection, researchers observed a distinct break in the scattering time series versus scale graph. This confirms selective sweeping and allows for the quantification of local wind speeds within the falling snow environment.

Deductive reasoning is essential for enabling robots to navigate through unknown environments. However, manually programming specific deduction rules for every potential scenario is labor-intensive and often impractical. To address this challenge, we introduce **Profound Active Deduction (PAD)**, a system capable of automatically learning both new deduction rules and their corresponding active actions from a robot's historical experience. By leveraging an action-embedded active deduction framework, PAD enables the robot to refine its reasoning capabilities independently over time. Experimental results across both simulated and real-world unknown mazes demonstrate that the robot equipped with PAD can deduce paths more effectively than existing methods, resulting in superior efficiency in exploration and navigation.

Three-dimensional Time Projection Chambers (TPCs) offer significant potential for future particle physics experiments by enabling comprehensive reconstruction of both particles' and antiparticles' spatial trajectories and kinematic properties. However, effective reconstruction demands sophisticated, computationally intensive processing of these vast datasets. To address this, we introduce a new data reduction strategy that leverages the spatial sparsity inherent in TPVs, combined with an asymmetric Convolutional Autoencoder (CAE) model. This approach was tested using simulated data from the Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer (AMS-2) for the upcoming COSMO-2 mission and the anticipated APEX detector. The findings demonstrate that the method successfully lowers memory requirements and accelerates processing speeds without sacrificing reconstruction accuracy.

The Finzi gravitational model, a classical statistical mechanics framework, offers a description of self-gravitating systems that aligns with observations of galaxy clusters. This study reports on new statistical analyses using the canonical ensemble to characterize systems with fixed total mass and energy. We examine distributions for various thermodynamic variables, calculate their moments, and investigate the statistical link between particle count and system energy. Additionally, we examine how changing the model's Finzi parameter alters these distributions and their underlying statistical properties.

This study introduces a new phenomenological model for calculating the differential cross-section of $\alpha$-particle production in the $^{6}$Li+$^{51}$V system, based on two-step reaction mechanisms. In the initial stage, $^{6}$Li decomposes into $\alpha$ and $t$ via cluster disintegration, while in the subsequent stage, single-nucleon pickup reactions occur where a neutron from the $t$ fragment picks up a proton from the target nucleus to form He-4. Furthermore, the model successfully reproduces the experimental ratio of $\sigma(\alpha+t)/\sigma(d+^3$He), which measures the relative probabilities of producing alpha-particle-plus-triton versus deuteron-plus-helium-4 outcomes.

This paper introduces a novel design for a reconfigurable FPGA system-on-module (SoM), named "Pacific Lamprey," named after the iconic regional fish species. The board utilizes an AMD Versal AC702 reconfigurable core, leveraging its heterogeneous compute resources to support multiple concurrent configurations. The proposed design features three distinct system designs—labeled as slow, medium, and fast modes—each utilizing a dedicated partial reconfiguration strategy. These modes utilize on-board DDR4 memory with speeds ranging from 1/4, 1/2, and all four channels respectively for partial reconfiguration. Evaluation results demonstrate a four-fold increase in bandwidth and a substantial boost in overall system performance. The design is open-source and accessible via https://github.com/UBC-ECE/pacific-lamprey.

Immuno-oncology seeks to bolster a patient's natural defenses against malignancies. This study investigates the most effective tailored therapies by modeling the human colon-cancer induced immune response, applying a Fokker-Planter approach to derive the joint probability density function of immune and tumor cell populations. Within an Itô stochastic environment, we establish boundary conditions representing either healthy or cancerous states and employ separation of variables to resolve the spatial-tempal probability distribution. Subsequently, we calculate the mean and variance for both tumor load and immune response strength. Finally, leveraging a Kullback-Leibler divergence metric, we determine the theoretically optimal ideal customized therapies aimed at maximizing immune system power against cancer.

Direct Device-to-Device (D2d) communication offers a promising solution for enhancing network capacity and data rates. However, the scheduling challenge in D2d networks is NP-hard, necessitating practical and efficient approaches. This study introduces a deep learning-based methodology for scheduling D2d connections, designed to maximize the system's throughput. Specifically, a deep neural network is employed to estimate the interference nulling potential between active D2d links and the cellular macro base station (MBS). Leveraging these interference estimates, a decision mechanism determines the scheduling of each D2d connection, aiming for maximum total network throughput. Extensive simulations validate the effectiveness of the proposed deep learning strategy.

We present a rigorous, analysis-based proof that small, barotropic perturbations of 2D flow with a positive constant background vorticity maintain hyperbolicity and smoothness indefinitely in time. Consequently, standard algebraic bounds on butterfly effects confirm that the classical Kelso-Bernstein-Caflisch (KBC) lower bound for the helicity threshold is optimal. Specifically, if the initial relative vorticity fluctuation amplitude is less than the inverse of the background vorticity magnitude, the 2D Euler evolution preserves the sign of the helicity regardless of how the spatial domain size scales. Assuming the standard KBC result, our result further implies that for the compressible Euler system, the previously established helicity threshold by KBC remains optimal.

This study employs post-Newtonian theory to investigate the residual eccentricity of eccentric gravitational-wave (GW) inspirals, which persists after they cross a GW detection threshold. We demonstrate that this residual value is largely determined by the observation threshold's signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) amplitude, denoted as $\mathcal{C}_0$. For an inspiral reaching a $\mathcal{C}_0 = 20$ signal, the initial eccentricity decays to approximately $10^{-4}$ post-observation, a value that is essentially independent of the eccentricity at which the signal enters the band. Furthermore, we find that the rate of eccentricity decay following the observation threshold depends on the initial eccentricity, ranging from $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-3}$ for signals beginning with eccentricities between $0.01$ and $0.1$.

The High Luminosity Coherent X-ray source (HLX) is a proposed facility designed to deliver high brightness coherent radiation across the 100 eV to 100 keV range. This source is achieved by amplifying X-ray free-electron lasers (XFELs) within a multi-stage system that includes a total energy regenerator (TER) and a cascaded Raman amplifier (CRA). To ensure stable operation and mitigate the TER's inherent risk of total lasing, a free-electron laser oscillator (FEO) is employed to condition the input seed pulses. This FEO generates narrow bandwidth pulses with high energy and coherence, which are subsequently injected into the CRA. The paper details the design of this FEO injection stage and analyzes its influence on the overall system's performance and output characteristics.

Accident detection in networks is crucial for maintaining service quality and reliability. While most existing research relies on historical data, this study examines accident detection using temporal networks that evolve over time. Our approach employs a holistic, data-driven technique to identify accidents by analyzing the structural characteristics of these evolving networks. We propose a new holistic feature, the Density-based Time Interval (DTI), to represent them. The proposed Holistic Structural Approach (HSA) utilizes Time Interval Density Evolution (TIDE) to capture how the network's density changes, and applies k-means clustering to identify distinct density patterns. These patterns are then matched to the actual subgraph representing the accident. We implemented the algorithm and conducted experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. The results demonstrate that HSA outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, achieving superior accuracy in detecting accidents.

In this study, we examine how a strong shock moves through a uniform, spherical, rotating gaseous medium that undergoes rotationally induced density variations. Our results indicate that in such a medium, density changes can be significantly reduced by the gaseous medium's rotationally induced density variations, effectively mitigating the adverse effects associated with density changes.

In the domain of machine learning, deep neural networks, and other sophisticated data-driven methodologies, the surging complexity has prompted researchers to explore "Explainable AI" (XAI) as a solution to the "black box" problem. While current XAI efforts predominantly originate from computer science, the field of requirements engineering (RE) can play a pivotal role in defining user-centric explainability specifications. This paper introduces a systematic approach to capturing user needs for explaining complex systems and demonstrates its utility through an industrial case study within the medical diagnostics industry.

We introduce "UniToPatho," a specialized database containing 1,000 H&E stained and whole-slide image sections of colorectal polyps, each annotated by expert pathologists with 22 distinct labels representing various histological characteristics. To maximize utility, every tag includes a confidence score and an identifier for the specific annotator. The collection is divided into 80% training data and 20% testing sets, with the latter featuring 100 unique, unseen sections to ensure a robust evaluation of any developed polyp analysis systems. The introduction of this resource aims to facilitate and enhance research and development efforts in colorectal cancer diagnostics and therapy.

A graph-theoretic framework is introduced to characterize data leakage in source encoding. Using graphs to model the dependencies between data sources, our approach provides a framework to model the dependency graphs of two specific leakage scenarios: an active scenario, where an adversary intentionally probes encoders, and a passive scenario, where an adversary observes encoders. Through this lens, we re-examine the fundamental problem of binary source encoding, analyzing optimal strategies for both active and passive attacks. Findings indicate that, for active attacks, an adversary can almost certainly deduce the complete view of all encoders with near certainty given just two observations. In contrast, for passive attacks, an adversary is restricted to information equivalent to direct observation of their chosen targets.

Deep generative models have proven highly effective for solving inverse problems, including SAR image super-resolution. This study introduces MrSARP, a hierarchical framework that employs two sequential deep generative models to iteratively refine super-resolved images. The initial model up-samples the low-resolution input, while the second model further enhances the resulting image. By introducing intermediate steps, MrSARP alleviates the information bottleneck inherent in single-stage approaches. Tested against single-stage baseline methods using the standard super-resolution benchmark, the proposed framework demonstrated superior performance.

The quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) represents a hybrid quantum-classical strategy for tackling combinatorial optimization challenges. In this framework, a quantum processor prepares a state parameterized for classical refinement via iterative loops. However, due to decoherence and quantum noise, the resulting probability distributions from classical measurements are often noisy, potentially hindering the convergence of these iterations. This work proposes a Bayesian refinement of the QAOA workflow designed to improve the quality of measured data. By utilizing posterior distributions to enhance data fidelity, our method reduces the total number of iterations required to identify high-quality approximate solutions. Numerical evaluations across several graph optimization problems validate the approach, demonstrating that the Bayesian improvement effectively boosts algorithmic performance.

This work addresses the determination of point sets constituting the intersection of two ellipses, each defined by a center, two semi-axes, and their corresponding orientations. While point-based intersection algorithms for ellipses are abundant in documentation, they remain scarce in open-source form. Consequently, this paper introduces an open-source Python implementation of such an algorithm, which was validated against high-performance existing methods published by multiple researchers. The findings demonstrate comparable accuracy and precision, with added advantages of enhanced readability and maintainability.

Adaptive methods for deep neural networks (DNns) have been a subject of debate, with critics arguing that they lack reproducibility and offer no theoretical advantages over standard optimizers. In response, we introduce "q-Training," an algorithm capable of integrating optimization techniques incrementally over time without downtraining existing components. Our approach is theoretically grounded, demonstrating the ability to adaptively lower the generalization error bound for specific data subsets while preserving the guarantees provided by baseline methods. The theoretical soundness of q-Training is complemented by experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets, which highlight the practical benefits of hybridizing optimization strategies.

We investigate an extended Hubbard model on a triangular lattice featuring nearest-neighbor hopping and nearest-neighbor Coulomb interactions. Employing the Dynamical Mean-Field Theory (DMFT) within the "two-band" approximation, we explore the low-energy physics across a broad range of interaction strengths. Our findings reveal that the system stabilizes into diverse states characterized by magnetic order, including collinear antiferromagnetism, stripe ferimagnetism, helical magnetism, and canted antiferromagnetism. Notably, non-collinear magnetic ordering emerges at intermediate interaction values, manifesting as both a stripe and a uniform helix. We map out a comprehensive phase diagram illustrating these varied magnetic configurations. Furthermore, we identify an order-by-disorder phenomenon where disordered fluctuations select specific ordered helical or stripe magnetic states from a pool of competing possibilities.

Vertebrae are critical landmarks for spinal disease diagnosis and treatment planning. However, existing CT-based methods that rely on vertebrae positioning and recognition often face challenges due to low image quality, sparse features, and inconsistent alignment. This paper introduces a new approach that automatically rectifies the spine and employs an anatomically constrained enhancement to generate high-quality vertebrae masks. First, the system automatically aligns and rectifies the spine within CT scans. Second, it utilizes these aligned spinal features to guide a U-Net model with anatomical constraints for generating precise vertebrae masks. This two-stage pipeline offers a robust solution for handling diverse scans, demonstrating significant improvements in both spine alignment and mask generation. Quantitative results indicate an average Dice coefficient of 0.89 and a Hausdorff Distance of 2.11 mm. Qualitative analysis further confirms that the rectification strategy effectively reduces variability in input masks, while the constrained enhancement ensures anatomically accurate and detailed segmentation.

We investigate stochastic Ising models on locally finite graphs where edge weights are randomly and independently selected from a uniform distribution on $[0,1]$. These weights govern a Brownian motion that drives a trajectory through configuration space, evolving a measure $\mu_t$ that tracks particle positions along the path. Our research focuses on the weak limit distribution of these measures $\mu_t$, a framework applicable to various dynamical systems such as ideal gases, zero-range processes, and Brownian motions influenced by random environments. A central finding is that the asymptotic behavior of these limit distributions remains gauge independent, a result that extends to scenarios involving non-uniform one-dimensional weight distributions and may find application in analyzing particle currents for specific systems.

For a symplectic manifold, we define relative quantum homology and demonstrate its long exact sequence connecting relative and quantum homologies of resolutions for symplectic singularities. Furthermore, we establish the connection of this relative framework with restriction quantum map, while also defining and examining the behavior of dual basis under coordinate transformations within rational symplectic spaces. Piezo crystals, which convert mechanical strain into electrical signals and vice versa, are extensively utilized in acoustics and are typically mounted on a common substrate. This study employs numerical simulations to demonstrate that a piezo crystal can entirely transmit generated acoustic waves to an adjacent crystal when they are positioned in close proximity on the same substrate. Numerical investigations reveal that this transmission results from mechanical strain propagation through the substrate, which is significantly more efficient than wave energy dissipation. Although the phenomenon is simulated using two-dimensional models, its applicability extends to three-dimensional scenarios. Consequently, this capability enables the interconversion of individual crystals to switch between energy storage modes: either as mechanical strain or as electrical energy within the crystal itself.

This study introduces an innovative optical approach utilizing liquid liquid exciton-polaritons in semiconductor microcavities as non-linear optical reservoirs. Within this framework, we demonstrate that a monochromatic pump beam can assemble liquid liquid exciton-polaritons into a coherent state, enabling the reservoir to function as a tunable, monochromatic source of light. We further propose that this assembly can serve as an adaptable frequency filter capable of selectively transmitting exciton-polaritons matching a specific energy. Finally, we illustrate that this system supports optical resonance states analogous to those found in traditional reservoir optics employing linear reservoirs.

The newly discovered ultra-short-period (USP) planet K2-22 b, orbiting the K2V star K2-22, has been identified as a primary target for investigating atmospheric erosion. This study presents the first detection of dust surrounding K2-22 b using the Gran Telescopio Canarias and the Multi-Object Mirror etTraction Camera (GMT/ETC). We employed a comprehensive model to analyze the data, revealing that the dust resides in a torus at a distance of 1.04 ± 0.04 R* (where R* is the stellar radius) with a vertical scale height of 0.16 ± 0.02 R*. The particles are characterized by radii between 0.1 and 10 μm, corresponding to a size distribution index of p = 3.5 ± 0.5. Assuming the dust originates from the disintegration of the planet, our calculations indicate a mass loss rate of 10^13 ± 0.5 g/s, which is a factor of 100 greater than typical values for hot Jupiters. This significant rate suggests that K2-22 b could vanish entirely within 100,000 years. The dust distribution is consistent with formation via the fragmentation of silicate particles, with sizes limited by the star's acoustic cutoff frequency.

We enhance the understanding of the fiber coherence of a local analytic fibration $f: (X,0) \to (\mathbb{C},0)$, where $(X,0)$ is a smooth complex germ, by demonstrating that the fiber cohomology groups $H^1(\mathcal{F}_t, \mathbb{C})$ vary locally constantly for a generic regular value $t \in \mathbb{C}$. This result follows from establishing the flatness of the crucial locus within the regular part of the discriminant, $cr(f): (X^{\rm reg},0) \to (\mathbb{C}^{\rm reg},0)$, thereby generalizing a prior finding by B. Banchoff and C. Souto. Additionally, we provide an upper bound for the Lefschetz number $\ell(\mathcal{F}_t, \mathbb{C})$ of the monodromy operator $\mathcal{F}_t$ on $H^*(\mathcal{F}_t, \mathbb{C})$, extending a theorem by J. Milnor that applies to holomorphic map germs.

This paper introduces Daany, a .NET-based data analysis framework designed to facilitate the development of data-driven applications. It offers a comprehensive suite of tools for data manipulation, including filtering, sorting, and mathematical operations, all built upon LINQ and collection methods. The framework supports both synchronous and asynchronous application styles, utilizing a design pattern that enables a seamless transition between these modes through simple, effective code refactoring. Additionally, the study presents a dual approach for developing functional test suites: one method employs standard xUnit and NUnit frameworks, while the other automatically generates and executes tests based on framework source code. This automatic generation process is achieved via Meta-Programming techniques within the application's existing code architecture.

This paper examines the life and work of Galileo, the renowned polymath, focusing on his pivotal role in the shift from philosophy to mathematics as the primary instrument for investigating nature. We demonstrate that, although often celebrated for his physical theories, Galileo's own insights into how to study the natural world were shaped more by his lesser-known studies in music and geometry. Consequently, analyzing his foundational concepts through the lens of these specific intellectual influences provides a clearer understanding of his scientific methodology.

Recombination dynamics within the primordial cosmos have been extensively investigated in light of CMB observations, notably regarding the impact of Saha equilibrium on primordial non-Gaussianity. This study introduces a novel analytical framework to examine Saha recombination, revealing that the Saha function exhibits a significant nonlinearity that cannot be approximated by simple linear models. We find this nonlinearity generates a substantial local-type primordial non-Gaussianity, with an amplitude of $f_{\rm NG} \sim 0.01$. This value is notably higher than the $f_{\rm NG} \sim 0.001$ derived from prior calculations, which relied on the oversimplified assumption of a linear Saha function. Our results indicate that the Saha function's nonlinearity could become the primary determinant of Saha-induced non-Gaussianity, surpassing contributions from perturbations in the photon-baryon fluid.

This study employs a hybrid model combining global magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) with local particle-in-cell (PIC) techniques to analyze magnetic island merging. By dynamically linking these approaches, we can efficiently simulate vast domains while capturing critical local details. Using this method to simulate the merging of two X-point configurations with comparable sizes, we observed that our model accurately reproduces experimental data regarding post-merging characteristics, specifically island size and 3D reconnection rates. Comparisons with pure MHD simulations reveal that the hybrid model offers superior accuracy in modeling reconnection rates. Furthermore, we identified that electron effects significantly influence the merging outcome, particularly by enhancing reconnection speeds.

Ammanuensis is an agent designed to work alongside human coders, capable of generating full Python functions given a set of input and output examples. Its training data consists of over 1.5 million function pairs sourced from public GitHub repositories. This system converts "few-shot" learning into a "many-shot" approach by treating each few-shot example block as a training sample, effectively enabling the model to learn vast numbers of examples efficiently. Empirical results demonstrate that only a small number of prompt examples are typically sufficient for optimal performance, as agents cease improving after surpassing this threshold. Furthermore, distinct from prior research that relies on refining static prompt selections, Ammanuensis dynamically learns prompts through few-shot training data. This dynamic learning process yields a significantly more capable coding agent compared to methods that merely search for or use specific prompt variations.
